#3635. Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir Knows How To Get Star Trek Back On Track [Exclusive]

Andy Weir, the author of the hit novels "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary," has seen the state of modern "Star Trek" and feels he knows how to fix it. In brief, he wants to get back to basics. In a new interview with /Film's Jeremy Mathai, Weir said he feels that the franchise should focus on making a TV series — not a movie — about a Starfleet vessel on a simple mission of exploration into deep space. No bells and whistles, no gimmicks. Just plain, baseline "Trek."

What does Weir mean by getting "Star Trek" back on track? Well, the franchise has experienced a lot of ups and downs throughout its 60-year history, and we're at a point where, many might agree, "Star Trek" became a little too ambitious for its own good. Starting in 2017, "Star Trek" churned out eight (!) original shows (nine, if you count "Very Short Treks"), and one TV movie. The two current Trek shows — "Strange New Worlds" and "Starfleet Academy" — will run their course next year. There are currently no new "Star Trek" shows in active production.

The franchise had an excellent run from 1987 through 2005 (the beginning of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" through the end of "Star Trek: Enterprise"), but by the end of that era, the saga had kind of petered out, and audiences had lost interest. "Star Trek" experienced a resurgence in 2009 with J.J. Abrams' reboot movie, and that carried through two hit sequels. That era, however, could never get its feet underneath it for a fourth movie, and that, too, petered out. Now the Paramount+ era is petering out as well.

Andy Weir thinks a single show about exploration might be the way forward.

In his interview with /Film, Andy Weir rightfully pointed out that "Star Trek" has always functioned best when it is a weekly, episodic TV series about varied adventures throughout the galaxy. Weir feels that making a new movie at this point would be unwise. He also notes that this proposed new series wouldn't have to rely on nostalgia, existing characters, or the USS Enterprise. To quote:

"[I]f I was the boss of 'Trek' [...], I would try to establish ... You've got to make a show, a series. I personally wouldn't try to go straight to films. I would go back to a series, a streaming show maybe that's just called 'Star Trek,' and then work from there. It doesn't have to be about the Enterprise. 'Star Trek' is a rich genre that has lots and lots of cool stuff in it. It could have that same feel. It could be about a different ship exploring strange new worlds and new civilizations."

Weir pointed out that "Star Trek" follows a specific DNA, which is, in his words, "this is a spaceship that goes out, finds new things, and has adventures." For him, "Star Trek" shouldn't aim higher than that, especially not after a decade of streaming shows that reached in all directions at once. The Paramount+ era has seen many shows taking place across the timeline of "Star Trek," with some being episodic and some being serialized. Some contain R-rated levels of violence, while others are aimed at toddlers. It's all too much.

Of course, the idea of a "Star Trek" series about a single starship, not the Enterprise, going on weekly adventures in deep space was the premise of 1995's "Star Trek: Voyager." Weir feels, though, that "Voyager" was not exactly what he means. He also thought that its immediate predecessor, "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine," while amazing, wasn't quite the "Star Trek" of a generation previous. Weir said that the original 1966 "Star Trek" made use of the franchise's DNA, as did "Next Generation," but after that, each show became a departure from the desired norm. He said:

"'Voyager' departed from it a little too much. People didn't like it. 'Deep Space Nine' had its own completely cool story. It was more of a political thriller, and they got away with it, but they didn't try to be 'Star Trek' with a slight twist. They're like, 'We're "Babylon 5." We're doing our own thing. We're doing it in the Star Trek universe, but we're doing our own thing.' So that's what I would do with Star Trek, is go back to the basics, go back to a ship exploring the cosmos."

"Babylon 5" is another sci-fi series, contemporaneous with "Deep Space Nine," that was also set on board a space station and that involved a lot of political intrigue. /Film loves "Deep Space Nine," but some people, like Weir, argue that it wasn't quite true to the Trek spirit. There wasn't enough trekking for his taste, one might suppose. But if the franchise did some simple star trekking, Weir would be happy.

With a new film in development, the folks in charge seem to be taking a different approach.

#3634. Commander Shepard’s Actors Are ‘Wildly Hopeful’ for Mass Effect, Despite Everything

‘Nobody has shut off the electricity because the community is the electricity’

EA shut down BioWare, laid off its staff, and canceled the in-development Mass Effect: Universe in October. That news sent shockwaves throughout the industry and through the communities that have sprung up around BioWare’s games. Mass Effect fans were hit particularly hard, and have started a petition to save Mass Effect. Some even purchased a time on a billboard in Times Square to advertise it.

Fans have tangled with a mix of emotions knowing that it’s unlikely they’ll ever get to play a new BioWare-developed Mass Effect again. But, if you ask the voices of Commander Shepard, they’re oddly optimistic about the future despite the circumstances. Polygon recently spoke to Mark Meer and Jennifer Hale, the voice actors for Shepard, about the strength of Mass Effect’s community, the closure of BioWare, and the studio’s legacy.

“My first response was sadness and concern for everybody who worked at Bioware,” Meer said.

After gutting the studio a year ago, EA laid off BioWare’s remaining around 50 employees on Oct. 21, bringing an end to its 30-year legacy. Meer noted that BioWare was a source of pride in Canada, and especially in Edmonton, where the studio was based. Canadian fans are even petitioning their government to save BioWare, and that petition will be presented in the House of Commons, meaning the Canadian government will formally address it in some way. “They were such a force in gaming and they were such a legend,” Meer said.

“BioWare was, in some beautiful, quiet ways, a very Canadian company,” Hale said. “Their games were inclusive. Their games bucked against tradition and [BioWare] did it their own way, quietly, but excellently. And they moved us forward, not by shouting and preaching, but simply by doing it in a very cool way.”

Hale was once overtaken by a wave of sadness about BioWare, but hers occurred some 20 years prior, when the studio was acquired by EA, which meant it became beholden to the whims and projections of shareholders and was no longer able to operate independently. EA’s 2025 sale to private investors, including Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, only further clashed with “the original spirit of BioWare,” as Hale put it. (BioWare reportedly was asked to remove LGBTQ-adjacent imagery from a video presentation, for example.)

“So, when I heard about the closure, I got wildly hopeful,” Hale said, acknowledging that optimism “sounds weird” at this moment. Like in her initial reaction to the closure, Hale described her optimistic vision for the future, one where EA is willing to part with the Mass Effect IP and that the fans “come together to own this IP as kind of a Mass Effect collective for the fans by the community, because there's some incredible devs in this community, incredible creators.”

Much has been made of if EA will sell off BioWare as a way of paying off the debt it’s taken on as a result of its sale. Though BioWare is closed, all its assets and franchises — from Mass Effect to Dragon Age to Jade Empire — still belong to EA. Former BioWare executive Mark Darrah thinks it’s possible EA could sell off BioWare IP, while former technical director Romain Toutain thinks it’s unlikely EA would sell anything. Regardless, that won’t stop people like Hale and Meer from hoping. “That was my dream that happened right away,” Hale said. “I like to hold onto the fiction that makes me feel good, because you never know.”

That’s a sentiment the community will surely share, especially as the shock of BioWare’s closure hasn’t completely gone away yet. Fans are still sharing their grief and love online, and the Shepards have noticed.

“The outpouring of love for those games, it was something to behold,” Meer said. He and Hale both support the #SaveMassEffect petition (which has more than 300,000 signatures), but noted they do not have any sort of organizational role in the campaign. “Ultimately, I think it's people showing that they're not really ready to let this universe go, and they would like to see more of it,” Meer said. “If it is just them showing how much it's meant to them, I think that's valid as well.”

All of this has happened on the eve of N7 Day, an annual celebration of all things Mass Effect that falls on Nov. 7. (Chosen because of Shepard’s in-universe N7 designation — it essentially means they’re the cream of the crop among humanity’s soldiers.) Cast members from Mass Effect have gathered on N7 Day the past few years, and this year will be no different.

“I don't think [N7 Day is] going to go away,” Meer said. “The fans have been doing it themselves for the last few years. So I think that you're going to see that continue.” He’s excited to see the fans post about Mass Effect, especially the cosplayers, and will gladly share them.

“Mass Effect hasn't needed a company behind it for a few years in order to have the kind of community power that it has,” Hale said. “Nobody has switched off the light or cut off the electricity, because the community is the electricity. Maybe there's not another game itself in development at the moment, but Mass Effect has a life of its own.”

Hale has been in the video games industry for decades, and acted in BioWare games even before Mass Effect, as did Meer. She’s seen how much things can change, and how the industry is currently in a cycle of corporations trying to get bigger and bigger. Companies are absorbing and purchasing each other at rates that are unprecedented compared to even a few years ago. “It's very hard to make creative turns” at the sizes they’re at, Hale said. She compared the current state of corporate culture to the mobile game Slither.io, where you play as a snake gobbling up other snakes until it becomes too large and easily dies. “And then all the little worms take over. It's kind of like that,” Hale said.

She’s hopeful indie studios will be those “little worms” rising up, and you can see some of that already. Mass Effect director Casey Hudson left BioWare years ago, and eventually co-founded Arcanaut Studios (also based in Edmonton). He’s directing Arcanaut’s upcoming Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic. Next year’s I-can’t-believe-it’s-not-Mass-Effect Exodus is the first game from Archetype Entertainment, a studio that’s home to several BioWare veterans.

Those games and more will carry the BioWare torch forward. “There is this real thirst for games that really have storytelling and a narrative,” Meer said. He named that rich storytelling and “characters that people really took into their hearts” as BioWare’s legacy. Because even if the studio is gone, the memories players made with characters like Garrus, Tali, Joker, Liara, and more aren’t.

“Things have their seasons,” Meer said. “Hopefully we shall see the season for Mass Effect again.”

#3633. How to Export Your Arc Data to a New Browser

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

#3632. Godzilla Minus Zero's Surprise Villain And Its Franchise History Explained

This article contains major spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

The King of the Monsters is back, and this time, he's not alone. Director Takashi Yamazaki has returned with a follow-up to his Oscar-winning smash hit "Godzilla Minus One" in the form of "Godzilla Minus Zero." Topping the film's predecessor was never going to be easy, but Yamazaki brought a not-so-secret weapon: King Ghidorah.

The King Ghidorah design for "Godzilla Minus Zero" leaked online thanks to merchandise, despite Toho trying to keep the monster's reveal a secret from the viewing public. But now, the cat is out of the bag, and this movie winds up being a showdown between Godzilla and one of his oldest foes. And much in the same way that Yamazaki reinvented Godzilla in "Minus One," he very much puts his own stamp on Ghidorah in "Minus Zero."

Anyone who has seen the sequel undoubtedly knows that King Ghidorah is a wildly powerful, foreboding kaiju. The design of the monster is very faithful to what fans of the franchise have known for years, but he's also modernized with some terrifying additions, including some wild new abilities that lead to some downright jaw-dropping action sequences. "Godzilla Minus Zero" is rated R, and that allows Yamazaki to not hold back in terms of the destruction and chaos caused by this hulking beast.

As even casual "Godzilla" fans are surely aware, this is far from the first time that Ghidorah has gone toe-to-toe with the King himself. So, in light of his latest appearance, it's worth looking back at the monster's history, how he's evolved over the years, and how this movie puts a new twist on him.

King Ghidorah first appeared on-screen in 1964's "Ghidorah, the "Three-Headed Monster," one of the best "Godzilla" movies of all time. By that point, the "Godzilla" franchise had become rather popular, and the titular monster was no longer alone. He'd faced off against Anguirus, King Kong, and Mothra. So, Ghidorah was far from the first kaiju battle for Godzilla, but he set a new high bar and instantly asserted himself as Godzilla's most powerful foe.

In terms of his origins, King Ghidorah is an alien monster who wiped out an alien race on Venus and came to Earth on a meteor. Ghidorah was such a formidable threat that the only way he could be defeated was to unite Godzilla, Mothra, and Rodan together against him. Ghidorah is truly one of the only monsters that might be scarier than Godzilla. This was essentially the first time that Godzilla went from villain to humanity's savior (although that line was already starting to blur by then).

Ghidorah quickly became a staple of the property. He re-appeared a year later in 1965's "Invasion of the Astro-Monster" and then again in 1968's "Destroy All Monsters," which features one of the most iconic "Godzilla" movie moments (Ghidorah getting stomped out by a group of kaiju). Ghidorah has since come back for every era of the franchise, including 1991's "Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah" during the Heisei era (which also introduced Mecha-King Ghidorah).

He later appeared in the Millennium era in 2001's chaotic "Godzilla, Mothra and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack" and in the MonsterVerse in 2019's "Godzilla: King of the Monsters." Rivaled perhaps only by Mothra, Ghidorah truly is Godzilla's most notorious foe. And where Mothra is often an ally, Ghidorah is as bad as they come.

On the one hand, Takashi Yamazaki is very faithful to King Ghidorah in "Godzilla Minus Zero." At the same time, though, he makes the monster feel fresh again with a terrifying makeover, one that fits in very well with the universe he set up in "Minus One." Ghidorah still shoots lightning bolts from his mouth, has that gold, scaly skin and those three dangerous heads, and remains massive. But there's an evolution to the kaiju here that makes this version particularly terrifying.

The very first scene of the movie shows us Ghidorah in a new form, namely what looks, for all intents and purposes, like a dragon with just one head. His design would be right at home in "Reign of Fire" (one of many fantasy movies that didn't deserve to flop at the box office). But I digress. After this initial attack, we learn that Ghidorah arrived on Earth via a meteor, keeping his alien origins intact.

Yamazaki's big change comes when Japan tries to kill a dormant Ghidorah. After dropping a bomb on him and impaling him so that he'll be struck with lightning, Ghidorah evolves into his final, more familiar form. The biggest change is his horrifying ability to use gravity beams, literally lifting towns into the sky and dropping them down to Earth.

The big climax relies on the film's humans forcing Godzilla to fight Ghidorah in a winner-take-all grudge match. Godzilla wins by blowing Ghidorah to pieces, but it isn't easy. The ending of "Godzilla Minus Zero" doesn't make it clear where the franchise goes from here, but it does leave some doors open. However, what isn't left dangling is any question as to who reigns supreme. At the end of the day, Godzilla is still the king.

Enter the retro-futuristic line of statement-making Nothing headphones. One of the brand’s popular pairs, the Nothing Headphone (1), is 33% off and down to $199 (originally $299), marking a record-low price.

The Nothing Headphone (1) pairs spatial head tracking audio with adaptive ANC, providing up to 80 hours of playback with ANC off and 35 hours with ANC on. A five-minute charge delivers up to five hours of playback, though this figure will vary based on volume and feature use. The headphones support Bluetooth multipoint, high-resolution LDAC, AAC, and SBC, but can also be played through a 3.5mm or USB-C cable. Volume is controlled using a scroll wheel, while pressable controls let you skip tracks. PCMag notes in their review that despite how distinctive the controls are, they’re easy to use.

Sound is adjustable using the presets and advanced equalizer in the Nothing app, and the ANC is reliable at neutralizing background noise. If you still want to remain aware of your surroundings, you can turn on transparency mode. Despite the unusual rectangular shape of the outer earcups, they’re round on the inside with ample padding and have an IP52 rating that can handle light splashes—but otherwise shouldn’t get wet.

While you can get stronger audio and ANC, you’ll be hard-pressed to find it at the $200 price point, often having to jump into the $400 range for premium options from Sony or Bose. Still, if you don’t mind fiddling with the EQ and your priorities are a cool-looking aesthetic and plush, sizable earcups, the Nothing Headphone (1) is worth considering.

Nearly thirty years later, There’s Something About Mary is widely regarded as one of the best remembered and most successful comedies to come out in the 1990s, but prior to its release, it wasn’t exactly considered a sure thing. In fact, its directors, The Farrelly Brothers, got locked into an extended power struggle with Fox before the cameras started rolling. The studio wanted two scenes removed from the shooting script. The Farrelly Brothers said no.

The standoff was so heated that the film apparently sat in pre-production for months. Eventually, Fox executives backed down and gave the filmmakers $23M to make their movie with the two scenes in question. They were, of course, the infamous zipper and hair gel scenes, and based at least partly on the outrageous nature of those two scenes, the film went on to gross nearly $400M at the global box office and was nominated for multiple Golden Globes.

CinemaBlend’s Riley Utley recently interviewed Peter Farrelly as part of the promotional day for his new film I Play Rocky, and he told her the story. Here’s a portion of his quote…

The bigger fight for us was Something About Mary, when you know the hair gel scene and the zipper scene. The studio is like, cut those and we'll greenlight your movie. I was like, no, those are the two funniest scenes in the movie. And they're like, we're not greenlighting it with those scenes in it. So we held out on that for six months. I said I don't want to make the movie and cut the two funny scenes. And luckily, they finally caved.

Now, you might be wondering why it took The Farrelly Brothers six months to get their way, especially given Ben Stiller and Cameron Diaz were interested in starring. They made Dumb & Dumber just a few years earlier, which was a massive hit and remains a cultural touchstone. They were the toast of Hollywood after their debut grossed almost $250M, but their follow-up, Kingpin, worked for some fans but did not do so well at the box office. It barely made back its budget, and there were concerns the Farrelly Brothers may have been one hit wonders.

Because of that, I get the apprehension from the studio to greenlight another project, but for the life of me, I have no idea why that apprehension would have had anything to do with cutting the zipper and hair gel scenes from the movie. They’re both over the top and utterly disgusting for different reasons, as the former involves a character getting his zipper stuck in the worst possible place and the latter, which still gets referenced today, involves using ejaculate as hair product, but they also quite obviously fit the overall tone of There’s Something About Mary. If an executive didn’t like those two scenes, it’s hard to imagine they’d enjoy the rest of the movie, which contains more than its fair share of sex, drugs, serial killers and violence toward the developmentally disabled.

Fortunately for both the filmmakers and the studio, There’s Something About Mary was shot as intended and has been making people laugh for decades. In recent years, Peter Farrelly has branched out on his own and started making some more serious films. Green Book, of course, won Best Picture, and his latest I Play Rocky is getting serious Oscar buzz, especially for lead Anthony Ippolito, who is fantastic as Sylvester Stallone. The latter opens this weekend and is worth checking out.

#3629. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3628. Godzilla Minus Zero Finally Explains How Noriko Survived Minus One

This article contains spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

One of the most anticipated sequels of the year is finally upon us. "Godzilla Minus Zero" is the follow-up to 2024's "Godzilla Minus One," with director Takashi Yamazaki returning to once again put his stamp on the legendary franchise. And since "Godzilla Minus One" was officially the first movie in the franchise to win an Oscar, the pressure is on.

Thus far, the first reactions to "Godzilla Minus Zero" have been glowing, so it's fair to say mission accomplished. A big reason for that is because Yamazaki picked up where he left off, centering the action on the same characters two years later as Japan attempts to dig itself out of the devastation left behind by Godzilla's attacks. Specifically, Ryûnosuke Kamiki is back as Kōichi Shikishima and Minami Hamabe is back as Noriko as they both try to build a life for their adopted daughter, Akiko (Sae Nagatani).

As viewers will surely recall, Noriko was left for dead after Godzilla annihilated the Ginza District in "Minus One," which is one of the worst things that Godzilla has ever done. Miraculously and somewhat inexplicably, Noriko survived the attack. Shikishima and Akiko reunited with her in the hospital at the very end of the movie, and all seemed well — or mostly well, anyway. Noriko had a very strange, scaly growth on her neck, implying that something was amiss.

One of the biggest questions viewers were left with was how in the heck Norkiko survived Godzilla's devastating blast. It seemed like it was just for the sake of giving the movie a happy ending. However, "Minus Zero" not only explains how Noriko survived, but uses that as a major plot device that the sequel hinges on.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" shows the horrifying aftermath of a kaiju attack like never before, revisiting key events from "Minus One" from new perspectives. One of these scenes explains how Noriko survived. We meet Dr. Ogata (Jun Kunimura), who treated Noriko after the attacks in 1947. He explains that there's no way this woman should have survived. She was on death's door — so much so that he told a nurse to leave her and tend to someone else.

Miraculously, the following day, she was breathing with a strong heartbeat. Within days of that, her wounds had all but disappeared, save for her eye. The explanation? Godzilla's G cells were infused into several survivors. These cells have regenerative properties, which explains why Noriko's terrible wounds healed. Unfortunately, it's not all good news.

Every other person who was infected with the G cells died, with scaly growths emerging from their skin. This explains the markings on Noriko's neck at the end of "Minus One." But she was also the only one who managed to live this long with the G cells in her body. Those G cells are later used to help lure Godzilla to the final battle with King Ghidorah, using Dr. Murakami's amplification device. Throughout the movie, Noriko says she doesn't have much time left, as the scaly growths continue to spread.

In retrospect, it's interesting that the happy ending in "Godzilla Minus One" almost didn't happen. That ending teed up much of the sequel's plot and some of the more harrowing scenes in the franchise. Whether or not Noriko survives much longer is an open-ended question, but at the very least, Takashi Yamazaki didn't merely save her for the sake of putting a nice bow on the previous movie. There was a meaningful, in-universe explanation for that decision.

#3627. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3626. Grand Theft Auto 6 Physical Copies Are Officially in the Wild

Code in box editions have started to arrive

With preloads for Grand Theft Auto 6 just around the corner, Rockstar Games has sent the code-in-box editions to retailers, so stores can deliver them to customers on time. Shipments have started to arrive, giving us a first look at the physical edition of Grand Theft Auto 6.

Fans who have pre-ordered Grand Theft Auto 6 can preload the game starting next week to ensure that they're able to launch it as soon as it's released in their region. PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X players who bought GTA 6 through their console's digital storefront can preload it starting Nov. 10 at midnight. However, those who ordered the code-in-box edition will have to wait until Thursday.

As players get ready to pick up their physical editions of GTA 6, local retailers have started preparing for the onslaught of gamers bound to rush to stores on Nov. 12. Shipments have seemingly arrived at MediaMarkt stores in Germany, and the retailer was quick to show the physical edition of Grand Theft Auto 6 on its Instagram stories. Thanks to this, we were able to get a first look at the poster that will be given to those who pre-ordered the game.

An employee also shared a close-up of the exterior of the box, revealing the official game description, screenshots of Jason, Lucia, and Leonida, and labels such as online support and in-game purchases. Players perked up at the thought of online support, though at this point, it likely refers to mini-game leaderboards rather than GTA Online.

We've known for months that GTA 6 is set to release on Nov. 19. Nevertheless, it's still hard for some to believe that launch day is nearly, finally here. The fact that people are now able to hold Grand Theft Auto 6 in their hands (even though physical editions don't actually include a disc) makes this whole thing feel even more real.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for Season 10, Episode 4 of 9-1-1, “Imposter Syndrome." You can stream it now with a Hulu subscription.

9-1-1 has always been anything but calm, and the season airing on the 2026 TV schedule continues that trend. One would think that after battling an active volcano and lava river, the 118 would have some downtime on their hands. However, for Buck, things got more chaotic with Theo, his biological son that he’s fostering. Honestly, I was shook over his parenting decision in the latest episode, too. However, Oliver Stark is clearing the air.

A few seasons ago, Buck had donated his sperm to his friend and his wife, who were having fertility issues. During Season 9, they both died in a car accident that the 118 were on the scene for, leaving Theo an orphan. In the Season 9 finale, Buck decided to take on the responsibility of foster parent, but he’s been having a tough time due to Theo’s behavior and lack of discipline. There was major concern for Buck going into Season 10, and while things haven't been all that bad, Thursday’s episode, “Imposter Syndrome," turned up the heat for him. That's because Buck got arrested after Theo threw a tantrum at the park and told cops that Buck wasn’t his father.

The situation made Buck rethink everything, and he came to the realization that Theo didn’t see him as a dad. After a brief fallout with Eddie over his parenting decisions, Buck talked with him about what happened and said that he can’t be Theo’s dad. Considering Buck’s persistence, I was shocked when he came to that conclusion; however, Stark told Us Weekly that it’s all part of Buck’s journey:

It’s important to remember that everything Buck is doing is with the best of intentions. He is making decisions day to day in this new role that he’s found himself in. He is always thinking it is the right decision and, obviously, we’ve seen it’s not always, and he’s struggling with it.

Anyone who has seen 9-1-1 knows that Buck does things with the best intentions. After seeing his friends die, he wanted to step up and care for their son, who just so happened to be his biological son. After all the trauma Theo went through, he probably just wanted to give him the best possible home he could, even if that meant having him run ragged and tearing the house apart. But that’s just what happens when you become a parent, as Stark shared:

As with any new parent, which is the role that he’s now in, you figure it out as you go. No one is immediately good at anything. You have to make some mistakes and you have to learn along the way, and that’s just part of the process that he’s currently in. It’s a particularly difficult situation. There’s a lot of trauma involved. I’m sure there is some level of guilt involved for Buck as well. He’s not necessarily making the right choices every step of the way, but he is making them with the best of intentions.

It’s been so great to see Buck’s evolution throughout 9-1-1’s run, because when the show was just starting, he was a rebel. He didn’t have a care in the world and was stealing fire trucks to have sex in them. Now he’s trying to step up as a father, and it’s a big change for him, especially after his parents revealed their divorce last season. It’s also a big change for Stark, who was excited to play out the story and see how Buck handles the whole thing:

Any apprehension that I had [about the storyline] when I first heard about it [vanished] after last season. I was fully on board, and I continue to be. I love working with the twins who played Theo. I’m really excited for the growth that it will mean for Buck — seeing him mirrored in so many ways and how it will make look at himself and how he can grow through that and how it can bring different characters in and out of his life. I just think it’s a big step for him, and I’m excited — very much so — about the storyline.

I, for one, have enjoyed seeing this side of Buck and watching how he is with Theo. It’s obvious he cares for him, and as Stark said, he has good intentions. While he definitely needs to change how he’s been parenting and be more strict, I think everything will turn out fine with him and Theo. Plus, it’s not like he doesn’t have a whole village to support him, even if he doesn’t listen to the tough love at first.

Overall, it sounds like this storyline will be sticking for quite some time, and I cannot wait to see what comes of it. New episodes of 9-1-1 air on Thursdays at 8 p.m. ET on ABC, streaming the next day on Hulu.

#3624. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3623. Godzilla Minus Zero's King Ghidorah Has One Scene That Was 55 Years In The Making

This article contains minor spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is here, with director Takashi Yamazaki once again getting to put his stamp on the King of the Monsters. He also got to offer up his take on another classic kaiju this time around in the form of King Ghidorah. The monster's appearance was a poorly kept secret, with Ghidorah's design in "Godzilla Minus Zero" leaking thanks to merchandise. But in any event, the monster's inclusion helped resolve a 55-year-old dream for the filmmaker.

According to Reuters, Yamazaki grew up in the Japanese ‌city of Matsumoto. A big "Godzilla" fan, he was particularly excited about 1964's "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster," one of the best "Godzilla" movies of all time. In particular, he hoped to see the kaiju wreck shop in his hometown. Unfortunately, Matsumoto only appeared fleetingly in the movie after Ghidorah's emergence.

Given that "Godzilla Minus One" became the highest-grossing Japanese Godzilla movie ever en route to winning an Oscar, Yamazaki was given a lot of creative freedom on the sequel. He used that freedom to show Ghidorah doing what he wanted to see as a child. "Minus Zero" prominently features Matsumoto, with Ghidorah carving a path of destruction there relatively early on in the movie's runtime. Here's what the filmmaker had to say about it:

"55 years later, I had King ‌Ghidorah ​appear in my own film. I had the chance ⁠to make the movie I ⁠wanted to watch back then, and I created the footage that I wanted to show my younger self, as if to say, 'This is what you wanted to see, isn't it?'"

"So, my dream has finally come true after ​55 years, and I am truly happy," Takashi Yamazaki concluded.

The sequel picks up two years after the events of "Minus One" as Japan is still trying to put itself back together in the aftermath of Godzilla's attacks. Things are once again thrown into chaos when a new, mysterious, dragon-like monster emerges. It's not long before Godzilla is back as well, leaving the people of Japan scrambling to figure out how to deal with not one but two kaiju.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is rated R, which meant that Yamazaki didn't have to hold back at all. When it came to having King Ghidorah destroy his hometown, he certainly made the most of that R rating. In a bizarre method of showing pride for the place he came from, he made the most of Matsumoto in his latest cinematic effort. Being from Japan and having your home shown off in a "Godzilla" movie is, understandably, something to be proud of.

King Ghidorah was the movie's "surprise" villain who has a long history with the franchise. "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" was his first of many, many appearances across the many eras of this franchise. In recent years, he's been showcased in everything from "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" in the MonsterVerse to the animated "Godzilla: The Planet Eater" on Netflix. He's without a doubt Godzilla's most notorious foe.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

#3622. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3621. I Love Christopher Nolan’s Robert Pattinson-Oriented Oppenheimer Story. Robert Downey Jr. Telling It Is Even Better

The inception, no pun intended, of Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer is quite the legendary tale at this point. This is probably because it involves the very buzzy and prolific actor Robert Pattinson planting the idea in Nolan’s head, despite having nothing to do with the movie. The director, characteristically, had a very matter-of-fact version of the story that people love. However, the way Robert Downey Jr. tells it makes it even better.

In an interview with Tara Hitchcock, Christopher Nolan talked about how he initially had an interest in J. Robert Oppenheimer and his role in American history. He specifically noted that a speech by Oppenheimer was actually used as a catalyst for Tenet and the way they wanted to tell that story. He said:

I wrote a thing about this incredible moment that Oppenheimer and the scientists of the Manhattan Project had, where they could not completely eliminate the possibility that when they triggered that first gadget – that first atomic device – they might start a chain reaction that would destroy the world. And we use that as a metaphor for Tenet, which Rob was in.

The Batman star recognized this interest, and by the end of the production, Pattinson decided to give Nolan a book of Oppenheimer’s speeches as a wrap gift on Tenet. Clearly, this interest in the speeches and the story had legs, as it helped inspire one of the best movies in the last decade and even led to a Best Picture win. I guess you can say that Robert Pattinson is really great at gifts.

In true Robert Downey Jr. fashion, the way he tells this story has its own special kind of energy. During his Actors on Actors interview with Mark Ruffalo, Downey told the tale like a fable, showing this gesture as a kindred energy between two creative men. He told Ruffalo (via Variety):

Pattinson gives him unwrapped Oppenheimer's letters—these moments in life where you realize the inception of something occurred in the most organic way. And also, Pattinson in Tenet was an incredible departure for him. So this incredible departure from one of our younger peers turns into him making a personal gift to arguably one of the greatest directors of—of his generation, turns into him deciding that it's sticking with him.

The way Downey tells it, it was a kinship moment. Robert Pattinson was seeing his career turn with Tenet, making him a more serious, sought-out character actor. And this made way for Nolan’s own transition, as he pivoted from tales based in sci-fi and action to one entrenched in the inner world of one of our most fabled historic figures. It was a world-stopping moment for two of our great creatives that went on to start a new and important chapter in both of their careers. It’s a beautiful way to put it, and it speaks to the storyteller that Downey is.

Pattinson may not have been in Oppenheimer and opted to do both Mickey 17 and The Batman instead; however, his impact on the Oscar-winning film is obvious. Clearly there was a connection with these two creatives, as Downey puts it, that made their separate careers flourish and then come together again for The Odyssey this year. It’s a great pairing, and I hope this partnership continues for years to come.

You can revisit Oppenheimer now, as it is currently streaming with a Peacock subscription. Christopher Nolan fans can also see him reunite with Robert Pattinson in The Odyssey, which is currently playing in select theaters around the country. It is one of the best films on the 2026 movie schedule, so make sure to check it out while you still can.

#3620. 5 Best New Movies And Shows To Stream This Weekend On Netflix, Apple TV, Hulu, And More (Nov. 6-8)

It's the first full weekend of November, the weather is finally turning truly chilly, and Halloweekend is in the rear-view mirror. Whether you went all-out on your costume last weekend or you elected to slap a nametag with a different moniker on your shirt and call it a day (which is my preferred way to celebrate Halloween if asked to do so), this weekend is perfect for staying in and curling up with a fresh series or movie. So, what's new on the big streamers?

Between Apple, Peacock, Hulu, and Netflix, there's a decent spate of new releases heading to streaming this weekend (and some of them even dropped earlier in the week). Whether you want to watch a gripping spy drama, a truly ridiculous legal drama, a breezy sports comedy, a crime thriller tinged with romance, or a quick-paced series featuring one of the best and weirdest pairings in TV history, I've got you covered.

Director Adam Carter Rehmeier, known for indie films like "Snack Shack" and "Dinner in America," teamed up with modern scream queen Samara Weaving and horror staple Kyle Gallner for this year's "Carolina Caroline" — which just hit Netflix, marking its first home on a major streaming service. Weaving, who also led "Ready or Not 2: Here I Come" and "Over Your Dead Body" recently (and who's joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe to play Emma Frost), stars as Caroline Daniels, a gas station attendant who falls in love with Gallner's con artist Oliver Anderson. As the two make their way to South Carolina from rural Texas, they end up committing robbery after robbery, leaving destruction in their wake.

Weaving's Caroline and Gallner's Oliver make for a great modern Bonnie and Clyde, and "Carolina Caroline" is a gripping, entertaining, and extraordinarily fun film that also features Jon Gries ("Napoleon Dynamite," "The White Lotus") and Kyra Sedgwick in supporting roles. If you want a crime drama packed with plenty of romance, "Carolina Caroline" on Netflix is your best bet.

Congratulations to all bad TV enjoyers: One of the worst shows ever made is back for Season 2! Ryan Murphy's gleefully ludicrous legal drama "All's Fair," which undoubtedly gives real lawyers raging headaches if they dare to tune in, stars Kim Kardashian as high-powered lawyer Allura Grant, who works alongside Liberty Ronson (Naomi Watts), Emerald J. Greene-Ball (Niecy Nash-Betts), Dina Standish (Glenn Close), and Milan (Teyana Taylor) at a firm that handles divorces. Sarah Paulson, a regular Murphy collaborator, livens up proceedings as rival lawyer Carrington "Carr" Lane, who is unbelievably twisted and extremely fun, and Nash-Betts, Watts, and Close are all game to ham it up.

I don't think I'm blowing anyone's mind when I say Kim Kardashian is a generationally dreadful actor who should not even appear in commercials, let alone a scripted drama that could be dishy and fun if she wasn't swanning around with absolutely zero expression in every single scene. Still, if you dig wildly bad TV and just want to switch your brain off, check out "All's Fair." Besides, if nothing else, it has given us an incredible episode of its fellow Hulu series "The Kardashians" where Close, out of character, gets very drunk off martinis at Kris Jenner's house.

I love "30 Rock," I have immense respect for weird little guy and short king Daniel Radcliffe, and I've been riding for Bobby Moynihan since the first time I saw him perform as Drunk Uncle on "Saturday Night Live." Essentially, "The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins" — which stars Tracy Morgan, was created by Robert Carlock and Sam Means, is executive produced by Tina Fey, and stars Morgan and Radcliffe as the unlikeliest and best duo in recent TV memory — was made for me in a lab. My enduring affection for this show aside, I think it's sure to delight pretty much anybody, and when Season 1 premiered in January, it immediately became one of the best shows of 2026.

The premise? Morgan plays Reggie Dinkins, a disgraced NFL star who was banned from the New York Jets and all other professional teams in the league after being caught betting on his games. (Hilariously, he only bet on his own performance to inspire himself to play better.) Thus, Reggie tries to regain his tattered reputation alongside his best friend and former teammate Rusty (Moynihan), his ex-wife and manager Monica (Erika Alexander), his young but extremely compatible fiancée Brina (Precious Joy), his son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall), and Radcliffe's Oscar-winning documentarian Arthur Tobin. With Arthur living in his palatial suburban New York mansion to make a documentary that will hopefully relaunch Reggie's career and get him into the NFL Hall of Fame, Reggie does his best to refurbish his image, and the results are extremely funny. "Reggie Dinkins" Season 2 dropped on NBC and Peacock on November 2, and if you're returning to this near-perfect series, welcome back. If you're new, go laugh your way through Season 1, then join us.

If you enjoyed Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw's delightful spy drama "Black Doves" when it dropped back on Netflix in 2024, you'll be pleased to hear the series — created by Joe Barton — released its second season on the streamer on November 5. Across six episodes, we pick up where the show left off with Helen Dawson (Knightley), a secret Black Doves operative who sells secrets to the highest bidder and also happens to be married to a Conservative MP for a major UK constituency and Secretary of State for Defense, Wallace Webb (Andrew Buchan). In the beginning of Season 1, Helen is shocked and saddened to learn that her lover, Jason Davies (Andre Koji), has died under suspicious circumstances ... and her secret identity may now be at risk.

Throughout that first season, Helen teams up with her old friend and hired assassin Sam Young (Whishaw), who's sent by the Doves to help protect her. In Season 2, after a shocking cliffhanger ending, we follow Helen and Sam as he desperately tries to keep her safe, even as she's targeted by nefarious forces throughout England. Knightley and Whishaw are fantastic together, and if you sort of forgot "Black Doves" was a thing since Season 1 premiered 2 years ago, I'm happy to tell you that it's back and still an extremely fun and enthralling watch.

Apple TV has some of the best comedy series on television hiding on its service (which seems to get overlooked in favor of ones like Netflix, Hulu, and Prime Video), and if you're a fan of "Ted Lasso" but haven't watched "Stick," you're really missing out. Owen Wilson leads this sports comedy created by Jason Keller and stars as Pryce Cahill, a former golf pro nicknamed "The Stick" who's stuck selling clubs and coaching at a country club after years of a career decline. At work one day, Pryce meets a gifted young golfer, Santi Wheeler (Peter Dager), who quit golfing after some personal issues got in the way of his game. Determined to make Santi the next golf star, Pryce ends up roping him into a cross-country tour to show off his talents alongside Santi's mother Elena (Mariana Treviño), Pryce's former caddy Mitts (Marc Maron), and a onetime bartender and current caddy Zero Duffy (Lili Kay), all of whom pile into an RV to make the trip.

"Stick" Season 2 adds great actors like Timothy Olyphant (as Pryce's former golf rival Clark Ross) as regulars and guest stars like recent Emmy winner Rhea Seehorn as Pryce's former coach, with Billy Zane also joining Season 2 in an as-yet-unknown capacity. The first two episodes of the sophomore season dropped on November 4, so catch up before it continues its run.

#3619. My Favorite Travel Headphones Are $250 Off Right Now

As a headphone reviewer, not many headphones outside of the flagship Sony, Bose, and Apple models get me excited. However, the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx headphones became the exception to that rule when I started using them over my Sony 1000XM6 as my go-to headphones. And right now, the Tour One M3s are down to $199.95 (originally $449.95), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools. This is a great deal for these headphones, which I deemed my favorite travel headphones in my review.

Everything from design to the features on the Tour One M3 was made with travel in mind. The headphones are very light, which, along with the comfortable soft earcups and headband, makes them great for wearing for long periods of time. I was able to wear these on a long flight without feeling any discomfort. Feeling like you're not wearing any headphones is the gold standard for comfort, and the Tour One M3 nails that aspect. The battery life is also impressive, with up to 70 hours with ANC off and 40 hours with it on.

The travel case is compact, convenient, and has extra storage for the audio transmitter, which is the best feature of the Tour One M3. This is a high-quality, low-latency audio transmitter. Anything that you can plug an AUX cable, USB, or USB-C port into can stream high-quality, 24-bit audio wirelessly to the Tour One M3. The main way most people will use these headphones is by plugging them into the in-flight entertainment, which lets you watch movies in high-quality LDAC with ANC. But I've also been able to use them to watch TV.

The Tour One M3 Smart Tx are incredible traveling headphones, especially at $199.95, and I recommend them to anyone who values comfort, battery life, simplicity, and likes the idea of the audio transmitter.
