#3618. I Wouldn’t Dream of Playing the Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Right Now

Some things are sacred. No, not like that!

Unlike you, probably, I am not playing Nintendo's Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time right now. I even turned down a kind offer from my editor to review it. This despite the fact that it might be my favorite Zelda game (mostly by virtue of being the first one I played) and indubitably one of the greatest games ever — as close to a Citizen Kane as the medium has.

I've read the ecstatic reviews, several of them by friends of mine, like Keza MacDonald and Christian Donlan, and of course Polygon's own Giovanni Colantonio, who I know to be people of good sense and great taste who share my reverence for this game and this series. I trust them.

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

I also trust Nintendo, especially now it's clear the game was developed by the in-house Zelda team and not farmed out to an external studio. I trust producers Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi, veterans of Zelda's golden age and architects of its great Breath of the Wild renaissance, who Gio talked to this week. I trust their decision to pass Ocarina on to younger developers at Nintendo to train and inspire them, but also to inject the aging game with youth and life.

Nintendo's top Legend of Zelda producers talk the remake, the future, and more

I also know that Ocarina needs the work. I played a little of the Nintendo 64 original recently, and while I remained entranced by its strangely haunted vibe, I found that, like so many early 3D games, it is fighting a battle with clunky, barely-ready technology that it has been slowly losing over the last 28 years. I'm honestly not sure that it's still fun to play now.

Zelda's most infamous dungeon is no longer a frustrating rite of passage

And this matters to me, because my 10-year-old son loves Zelda — which, to him, means Tears of the Kingdom. He thinks Tears is the best game ever, and I wouldn't necessarily disagree. He's read the Ocarina of Time manga and fiddled about with other games in the series, including the Link's Awakening remake and The Wind Waker, but never settled into any of them. Honestly, I warned him off trying to play the original Ocarina.

So the Ocarina remake arrives at a perfect time for him. He is beyond excited about it. He will get it, and his own Switch 2 to play it on, for Christmas. Put yourself in his shoes. (Maybe you once were, and got the original Ocarina, or the 3DS version, as a childhood Christmas gift yourself.) Can you imagine anything better?

I just know that if I played the game before him, even surreptitiously, I would be stealing the magic of that moment. As desperate as I am to see the work of Aonuma and Fujibayashi's team, I can't countenance it. So I'll wait with him.

Also… If I'm honest, maybe I'm not just doing it for him. Because I'll be unwrapping my own copy on Christmas morning. I'll be playing this magical game away from work, out of step with the discourse, in the cozy, contented, quiet bubble of the holidays, surrounded by my family. Maybe I'll feel like I'm 10, too. Like I said: can you imagine anything better?

ZA/UM, the makers of Disco Elysium — well, some of them; it's complicated — return with another wonderfully funny, dark, and emotionally complex narrative RPG that uses tabletop dice rolls to enumerate the failings of human beings. One in particular: a not good, very bad spy who is trying to atone for a terrible betrayal.

Disco Elysium follow-up Zero Parades has serious staying power

This 1988 NES classic from Capcom is simply one of the all-time great action platformers. It's all the more remarkable since the developers basically had to cobble it together in their spare time after the original was deemed a sales disappointment. Now Mega Man is a treasured franchise, and due for a return next year.

I'm not playing Ocarina, but I am allowed to listen to the eight-track soundtrack sample that just dropped on Nintendo Music, and it's absolutely delicious. The exquisitely produced and performed new arrangements of Koji Kondo's immortal tunes are both a massive upgrade and resounding proof that Kondo had loaded his music with all this drama, humor, and sophistication from the start. Impossible to pick a favorite from the full flamenco of "Gerudo Valley," or the squawking penny whistles, accordions, oboes, and fiddles of "Market," or "Kakariko Village"'s plangeant harmonica. But let's go with the 10-minute "Hyrule Field Main Theme" for sheer epic sweep.

It’s from the Deku Trio, because of course it is

#3617. 5 Years Ago: Benedict Cumberbatch Starred In Netflix's Best Western Movie

Jane Campion's 2021 film "The Power of the Dog," released five years ago this month, was one of the best films of its year. It was widely praised by critics and by the Academy, despite earning a tiny handful of cash during its not-very-wide theatrical release. The film was nominated for an astonishing 12 Academy Awards, including Best Picture, making it the seventh Netflix film in four years to be nominated in the top category (other nominees included "Roma," "The Irishman," "Marriage Story," "Mank," "The Trial of the Chicago 7," and "Don't Look Up"). "The Power of the Dog" ultimately only won one Oscar, for Best Director.

The film takes place on a ranch in Montana in the mid-1920s, owned by brothers Phil and George Burbank (Benedict Cumberbatch and Jesse Plemons). Kirsten Dunst plays Rose, the proprietress of a local inn, who is raising her teenage son Peter (Kodi Smit-McPhee) by herself. Early in the film, Phil admires that Rose's dining tables are decorated with paper flowers, but becomes a little grossed out when he learns that Peter was the one who constructed them. This little observation kicks off the movie's powerful themes about traditional masculinity, gender dynamics, and the place of queerness on the open frontier.

These four characters get swirled together when George marries Rose and Phil's cruel nature reveals itself. While the young Peter leaves to go to medical school, Rose finds herself under pressure — more from Phil than from George — to be a "woman of the house." Phil insists, for instance, that Rose play the piano at a fancy dinner party, something she can't bear to do. By the time Peter comes home for a break, Rose has begun to hit the bottle.

We soon learn that both Phil and the young Peter are likely queer. Peter is more openly so, as he becomes fascinated by a secret stash of magazines full of hunky dudes. Phil, meanwhile, is very fond of a scarf that once belonged to the now-dead Bronco Henry, his former mentor ... and possibly more. Eventually, Phil begins to take Peter under his wing. Later in the film, Phil tacitly admits that Bronco Henry once saved his life during a blizzard by holding their nude bodies together. It's all but stated outright that Phil and Bronco Henry were lovers. This is the 1920s in rural Montana, however, so these men don't seem to have the freedom, nor even the vocabulary, to express their queerness.

At home, meanwhile, Rose's life is falling apart. She's drinking more and more, and her relationship with Phil is fraught. Although Phil eventually warms to Peter, he seems to place all his self-hate onto Rose, mocking her and making her life as miserable as possible. Phil is blaming Rose, it seems, for forcing him to reckon with his attraction to men. This leads to a late-film twist about rope-making and anthrax that leaves the film on a very dark note indeed.

"The Power of the Dog" is a marvelous tragedy of pain, self-denial, and gender roles. Rose cannot be the "sweet little wife," and Phil masks his need to be gentle and "soft" by affecting a "grizzled" exterior. Cumberbatch is fantastic in the role of Phil, capturing both his character's cruelty and his hidden gentleness. The film's title comes from Psalms, 22:20: "Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs."

Jane Campion's filmography is full of bangers, going back to her early films like "Sweetie" and "An Angel at My Table," through "The Piano" and "Portrait of a Lady," and up to "Bright Star" and "The Power of the Dog." This has been her most recent film to date.

Critics loved this movie, which earned a 94% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes based on 363 reviews. /Film wrote that Cumberbatch delivered a career-best performance. Meanwhile, The New York Times' Manohla Dargis loved the sweep of the film as well as its treatment of the Phil character, a man who, she observed, had been "playing" a cowboy for decades of his life. About the film's visuals, Dargis wrote:

"A bold visual stylist, Campion introduces this world and its people with sweep and precision, with soaring eagle-eye aerial shots and her characteristic attention to voluptuary detail (and with New Zealand doubling for an unspoiled Montana). She fluently sets the western milieu, with its swirling dust and thundering cattle, and catches the boisterous camaraderie of the ranch hands, the playfulness of their jostling with its easy, unselfconscious physicality and intimacy."

/Film's Joshua Meyer wrote a full explanation of the ending of "The Power of the Dog," realizing that it's a tale of emotional terrorism and that it may be freeing to wriggle out from under the masculine lifestyle Phil was trying to perpetuate. "The Power of the Dog" was based on the novel by Thomas Savage, and Campion, who also wrote the adaptation, changed the ending (we think for the better). In Campion's version, the themes are incredibly clear, very moving, and pointedly righteous.

60 Minutes underwent a major creative overhaul this past summer, which saw executive producer Nick Bilton and CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss make considerable staff changes. Several notable series alums were fired and, since then, several new employees have been added. However, when the show returned for Season 59 as part of the 2026 TV schedule, some familiar faces were still on the air, including host Lesley Stahl. Now, Stahl is getting candid about remaining with the show under Weiss’ leadership after the firings.

Stahl – who’s been with 60 Minutes since 1991 – opted to remain with the news magazine program alongside fellow series veterans Bill Whitaker and Jon Wertheim. Ahead of the trio jointly confirming their decision to stay, there had been considerable speculation about their plans. Stahl spoke about her choice while being honored at the Power 100 luncheon this past week and claimed that she’d been on the receiving end of backlash for staying with the show. Via The New York Post, Stahl explained why she and her colleagues chose to stay:

I myself have been under attack on social media because of my decision to stay at ’60 Minutes’ under the new regime. It was not an easy decision. It was one I made with my colleagues Bill Whitaker and John Wertheim. There was an urge to walk out and protest in solidarity with our colleagues who had been abruptly and cruelly fired. But we decided to stay out of a fear, a fear that if we didn’t, ’60 Minutes’ would vanish.

60 Minutes Alum On The Show’s Bari Weiss Era And One Thing She Still Finds ‘Disturbing’

On May 28, which has reportedly since been deemed “Black Thursday" within CBS News, 60 Minutes correspondents Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi were fired alongside others like series EP Tanya Simon and executive editor Draggan Mihailovich. Days later, longtime correspondent Scott Pelley was fired as well after reportedly accusing Bari Weiss of “murdering” the show. In the months since then, Pelley, Vega and others have made claims of editorial interference against Weiss and claimed they were asked to exude bias in their reporting.

Bari Weiss herself has been at the center of backlash as well due to the claims of journalistic partiality. At this point, the Free Press founder has denied the assertions and emphasized her intention to improve 60. Since the show returned in September, ratings have reportedly been under the average of the previous season. Weiss addressed those concerns during a recent conference and stated that the series was doing “tremendously well.” Stahl also addressed that decrease in viewership while speaking at the luncheon:

Many loyal viewers over the last 58 years have tuned us out, we presume, in protest. To those who stopped watching, I’m asking you please to come back.

Back in June, Stahl discussed the state of 60 Minutes back in June. She addressed the wave of firings and referred to the fallout as the “hardest chapter” of her career. Stahl – who’s been in journalism for over 50 years – also said the series of firings “was by far the worst experience I’ve been involved in, or even witnessed.” At the time, Stahl also said she’d met with Bilton to stress that while she and her colleagues understood that more needed to be done to the show, she hoped that the broadcast wouldn’t be “tampered with.”

Since then, Bari Weiss and Nick Bilton have added Ross Douthat, Gianna Toboni, Trevor Phillips and Sebastian Junger in host and correspondent roles for 60 Minutes. Lesley Stahl’s future on the news program beyond this current season remains uncertain. In any case, it’s evident that a new era is currently taking shape not just at 60 but at CBS News as a whole.

#3614. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3613. 23 Years Later, Buddy The Elf's Best Line Is Still The Greatest Christmas Quote Ever

When "Elf" came out in 2003, it established itself as an immediate Christmas classic, and on the movie's 23rd anniversary, we want to celebrate a simple, effective line from this Will Ferrell comedy which is not only fun for the whole family, but which has stood the test of time.

Before we get to the line in question, though, let's go over the basics where "Elf" is concerned. Directed by Jon Favreau (the Marvel and Star Wars one, not the political guy) and written by David Berenbaum, who wrote the movie after an earlier project called "Christmas in New Jersey" failed to take flight, "Elf" stars Ferrell as Buddy the titular elf, a human who's raised at the North Pole by his adoptive elf dad, Papa Elf (Bob Newhart, who also narrates the film). When Buddy sets out to find his birth father on the magical, mystical island of Manhattan, he meets Walter Hobbs (James Caan), a cynical and uptight publisher of children's books who isn't super interested in dealing with any large adult son, let alone one dressed like a Christmas elf who pours sugar on his spaghetti. Thankfully, Walter's wife and son, Emily and Michael (Mary Steenburgen and Daniel Tay), love Buddy, so he's accepted into the Hobbs household and ends up saving Christmas.

There are a lot of great "Elf" quotes — and we'll feature a bunch of them shortly — but the one I really want to center is one that expresses Buddy's worldview perfectly. So what is it?

While talking to his coworker and eventual girlfriend Jovie (Zooey Deschanel), Buddy, trying to get her to sing in public, tells her, "The best way to spread Christmas cheer is singing loud for all to hear." Not only is this just a nice, neat little rhyme, it's also the entire essence of the movie.

Sure, Buddy can be annoying, loud, and weird; a grown man in an elf costume is a concept that's great on screen and would be objectively terrifying in real life. (It adds to the cinematic hilarity and imagined real-life horror that Will Ferrell is well over six feet tall.) Still, Buddy's big heart and intense joy ends up making everyone believe in the magic of the holiday season — even Walter, who eventually accepts Buddy as his son and decides that he wants to spend more time with Emily and Michael in the process.

"Elf" is truly a movie about allowing yourself to indulge in joy and cheer, and this Buddy quote is basically the film's thesis. That's not the only quotable line from "Elf," though; there are so many others.

#3611. One Of Daredevil's Most Important Characters Was Only Supposed To Appear Once

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

If you asked Marvel readers to name Daredevil's most important supporting character, many would answer Elektra Natchios, the sai-wielding ninja assassin and Matt Murdock's sometimes lover, sometimes foe. But she came fairly late into the publication of "Daredevil." Created by writer/artist Frank Miller, Elektra debuted in 1980's "Daredevil" #168. The issue details her past of falling in love with Matt in college. In the present, the two are reunited because Elektra's assassin job brings her into conflict with Daredevil.

Miller had been drawing "Daredevil" since issue #158. He asked "Daredevil" editor Dennis O'Neil for a chance to write the book, and he turned it around completely. Miller transformed "Daredevil" from one of Marvel's least popular comics into one of its best, as his hard-boiled writing and dynamic action made "Daredevil" feel unlike any other comic. (Miller soon did a similarly influential revamp of Batman, which is why Batman and Daredevil remain so similar.)

"Daredevil" #168 was Miller's first solo writing credit on the book. His cover (inked by Klaus Janson) depicts a lightning strike, a fitting image for what Miller would do for the comic. That lightning conceals Elektra in shadow, while Daredevil looks on in horror. "Once he loved her... now she is his most deadly enemy!" the cover declares. Between the cover's imagery and the story promised by that caption, how could you not pick up this comic?

But at the time, Miller didn't see Elektra as the key to overhauling "Daredevil." In a 1983 discussion with Comics Interview magazine, Miller explained, "I came onto ['Daredevil'] thinking I was doing a couple of fill-ins on the writing. I ended up taking over the series, [and] had a character who was only supposed to appear for an issue take over the series on me — Elektra."

Frank Miller named Elektra after the Greek myth of Electra, the daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra who killed her mother to avenge Clytemnestra's murder of Agamemnon. Elektra Natchios is also defined by the death of her father, a Greek ambassador murdered in a hostage situation during Matt and Elektra's college years romance.

"Daredevil" by Miller takes a lot from film noir, and an alluring but deadly woman from the hero's past is a noir hallmark. Miller had one particular noir story in mind: Will Eisner's crime comic strip "The Spirit," particularly a 1950 story that introduced Sand Saref, the Spirit's childhood girlfriend turned femme fatale. Elektra's backstory — in love with the hero, rejects the law after her father dies, becomes an international criminal — hits the same beats as Sand's. (Bringing this full circle, Miller directed a "Spirit" movie in 2008 featuring Eva Mendes as Sand Saref, but it received very bad reviews.)

In the 2003 documentary "The Men Without Fear: Creating Daredevil," Miller recalled that he had wanted to introduce a new type of superhero love interest with Elektra, i.e. one who jumps across rooftops with her man. "Why wouldn't [superheroes] be operatic in their romance the way they are in combat?" Miller asked.

Knowing Miller apparently thought he might get one chance to tell Elektra's story, it makes sense that "Daredevil" #168 tells a complete and tragic arc. Daredevil and Elektra clash over the same quarry, and Matt remembers his past with Elektra (a blatant retcon, one smoothed over by Matt's inner dialogue suggesting it's been too painful to think of Elektra since). The issue ends with Daredevil revealing he's Matt Murdock to Elektra, but they still live in different worlds now. He then vanishes into the night, leaving Elektra crying alone.

Frank Miller actually brought Elektra back in his very next issue, "Daredevil" #169, but that appearance writes her out. She enters Matt's apartment, sees he's involved with Heather Glenn, and leaves, once more heartbroken. As Miller settled in on "Daredevil," though, he brought Elektra back in issue #174 as a regular character.

From there, she fought alongside Daredevil against the evil ninja cult the Hand and was hired to kill her lover by Wilson Fisk, the Kingpin. Fisk's former assassin, Bullseye, didn't take kindly to being replaced, so he murders Elektra in the double-length "Daredevil" #181. Elektra's fate echoes previous deaths of Marvel Comics female leads (now called "fridging"), like Gwen Stacy in "Amazing Spider-Man" or Jean Grey in "X-Men."

Miller felt that Elektra had to die or else she'd become an "insipid character," and he managed to convince Marvel's reluctant then editor-in-chief, Jim Shooter. But in Miller's penultimate issue, "Daredevil" #190, Elektra is revived by the Hand — unbeknownst to Matt, who still believes Elektra lost to him.

Elektra's resurrection opened the door for her to return, like in Miller and Bill Sienkiewicz's "Elektra: Assassin" or Miller's "Elektra Lives Again." Miller later revised Matt and Elektra's past in the 1993 miniseries "Daredevil: Man Without Fear" (drawn by John Romita Jr.), retconning Elektra into a dangerous thrill-seeker from the start.

Nowadays, Elektra sits as a permanent fixture of Daredevil's world, played in live-action by Jennifer Garner and later Elodie Yung. The comic Elektra even became Daredevil herself during writer Chip Zdarsky's run on "Daredevil." That endurance is not what Miller had wanted, and he admitted Elektra slipping through his hands "stings like hell" in "Marvel Comics: The Untold Story." If there's one publisher that won't let a good character go, after all, it's Marvel Comics.

Michaelis' Runa is the breakout star of Zero Company

Dropout star Vic Michaelis used to fall asleep to Attack of the Clones. Not because they hated it, like so many Star Wars prequel detractors, but because it was their comfort watch. “I've seen the first 45 minutes of Episode II, I want to say, 300 times,” Michaelis told Polygon. “It's so comforting. The prequels hold a place in my heart where it is like nothing bad can happen when I'm watching them.”

Michaelis has now gone from watching Star Wars to being a part of the larger Star Wars universe. In Star Wars Zero Company, they played breakout character Runa Blask, the wise-cracking advisor to the titular mercenary group, led by Captain Hawks.

Michaelis hails from the improv comedy world, but they’ve done film and scripted TV shows as well. Zero Company was their first-ever video game role. “I was so simultaneously terrified, obviously, of the video game aspect of it and also, you know, the Star Wars of it all.”

Turns out, that fear was unnecessary. The team at Bit Reactor was familiar with Michaelis’ Dropout work, and that was part of the reason they wanted Michaelis for the role.

Their improv background helped influence their performance, though they weren’t changing lines or jokes. “The improv is so much about the preparation in a way that I think people don't really know.” Instead, all of Runa’s best quips were already in the very strong script. “All of my favorite lines that Runa had were written or pitched lines from the writers,” Michaelis said.

Among those lines were many instances of Runa saying “wizard,” which basically means “cool” in Star Wars. “Runa's very tall, everything is ‘wizard,’” Michaelis said with a laugh, joking they must have said the word “500 times.”

Fans have glommed onto Runa for her constant jokes and ribbing of Hawks. “I'm seeing a lot of people being like, ‘Runa, I love her, and I wanna throw her out a window.’ Which I really resonate with, and I think was part of what we were going for,” Michaelis said. “Big sister vibes.”

Runa can’t be thrown out a window. She actually can’t be harmed at all. While the game features a permadeath feature for its operators, Runa doesn’t go on combat missions and doesn’t leave The Den, Zero Company’s headquarters.

“I did start seeing people devastated and heartbroken that some characters that they put a lot of time and energy into didn't make it through,” Michaelis said. “Do I wish people sort of mourned me in that way? Maybe. I don't know. I’m going to be thinking about that.”

Before Runa was a member of Zero Company, she was a self-described “freelance consultant to the top corporations and families in the galaxy.” AKA, a Separatist financial fixer. She desires a fortune that working for Zero Company will never grant her. As she tells Hawks, if she had that fortune, she’d want to buy a moon and run a resort. Michaelis has much humbler aspirations if they were to live in the world of Star Wars. “I would want to be a small business owner,” Michaelis said, and started describing what would make for a very fun Disney Plus show.

“I want to do a comedy night at my bookstore and all of a sudden, you've got a bunch of interplanetary politics or some red tape of why I can't do this. Then I'm marching up to the Republic with my civil city ordinances, trying to get this comedy night happening, and I'm accidentally now involved and implicated in a sort of a greater plot,” Michaelis said. “And all I wanted to do was try and get a couple of standups at my bookstore at night so I could sell wine after hours.”

If Star Trek can have a critically acclaimed animated sitcom, why can’t Star Wars have a series about a store owner just trying to get a comedy night off the ground? Your move, Disney.

There’s no question that when Sydney Sweeney releases an ad campaign, it gets people talking. Whether it's selling soap infused with her bathwater, starring in an ad for American Eagle that led to serious backlash, or becoming an equity partner in Novig and doing an ad where she wore nothing but footballs, she knows how to make a viral moment. However, while these instances burn big and bright for a moment, do they actually turn into long-term sales? Let's talk about it.

When Sweeney’s first campaign with American Eagle launched, it was met with an intense amount of discourse. While it faced serious backlash, as some thought the campaign was promoting eugenics based on how it used the word “jeans” like “genes,” it did bring in 790,000 new customers in six weeks, and in Q3 of 2025, sales grew 1% according to Adweek. It also reportedly added about $400 million in market value and upped web traffic by 100%.

Then, after both Sweeney and Travis Kelce’s AE campaigns launched, there was a growth in sales around the holiday, as American Eagle Outfitters reported “record holiday-quarter sales of $1.8 billion.”

While Sweeney’s first campaign with American Eagle was a very big deal and did make an impact, the second did not lead to the same kind of gains. In this new report, it’s stated that in Q1 of 2026, AE’s sales fell 2% (even though total comps rose to 8% due to a 25% jump from the brand Aeire). In reference to that, Jay Schottenstein, the CEO of AEO, said that the overall results were mixed.

Michael Gunther, Consumer Edge’s SVP of Research and Market Intelligence, explained that when it comes to American Eagle’s second campaign with Sweeney, there’s “little evidence of a sustained improvement comparable to the original campaign’s holiday performance.”

Overall, it would seem that Sweeney’s campaigns do generate sales. However, once the shock of her ads wears off, sales dwindle. For example, when her Dr. Squatch ad about her bathwater came out, it “drove a 20% week-over-week jump in revenue,” according to the brand’s then-VP of Global Marketing, John Ludeke. However, in the months after that, Consumer Edge’s card data showed that Dr. Squatch’s slice of this market went down by 25 basis points.

It was also reported that while the brand sees double-digit growth in its future, it has seen a slowdown in bar soap sales. Dr. Squatch’s CEO, Josh Friedman, did make it clear, however, that Sweeney’s ad campaign was also successful because it ultimately helped the brand launch a body wash line.

As for the actress’ latest ad campaign with Novig, which did cause backlash, it’s had some notable early wins. Novig has raised funding at a $2 billion valuation, which is up from the $500 million it was at earlier this year. Along with that, first-time despitores went up over 281% in the weeks after Sweeney’s ad premiered. So, things are looking up for this partnership; the question is, can it be sustained?

The data seems to say her work provides sales in the short term. The long term is a bit of a different situation. However, if there’s one thing that’s certain, it’s that getting Sydney Sweeney in an ad is sure to generate a big conversation.

#3607. 5 Best Western Movies That Take Place In One Location

From Alfred Hitchcock's "Rope" to Sidney Lumet's "12 Angry Men," some of the best movies ever made have taken place in a single location. Limiting a film's scope in such a way is an extremely effective method for distilling the artform down to its most essential parts: character and storytelling. That's no different with Westerns.

Western movies have often taken advantage of America's incredible landscapes. From the genre defining Western (that barely impacted the box office) "The Big Trail" to the similarly decade-spanning tale of the Prescott family in "How the West Was Won," Western filmmakers have frequently made the land on which the United States was built as a big a character as the people themselves.

But some of the best Western films ever made have also unfolded on a much smaller scale — usually a frontier town where the clash between lawlessness and civilization can play out in microcosm. We've even seen Westerns confined to a single room. Regardless, placing limits like these on any film often brings out the best in its creators, and that's certainly been the case for this list of the best Westerns that take place in one location.

If you're going to make a movie set in one location, why not make it hell? That is, why not set it in a Western small town that may or may not be a physical manifestation of the underworld? The movie that prompted John Wayne to write an angry letter to Clint Eastwood was a fairly modest affair — at least in terms of its scope. 1973's "High Plains Drifter" sees Eastwood once again saddle up as a mysterious stranger. But this particular version of the Western archetype that Eastwood plays is less an anti-hero and more a manifestation of otherworldly retribution, who arrives in the town of Lago, ostensibly to protect its residents. In reality, he's there to make them pay for their sins.

One of many Westerns directed by Eastwood, "High Plains Drifter" is set almost entirely within Lago, where the townspeople allow outlaws to whip a U.S. Marshal to death. Eastwood's ghostly gunslinger then emerges from the surrounding desert embodying a cosmic fury as unforgiving as the parched plains from which he arrived. His order to paint every building in Lago red is designed as a way to depict the shame which covers the townspeople, and it's one of the most striking images in all of Eastwood's filmography.

Eastwood is no stranger to more grandiose depictions of the Old West. But "High Plains Drifter" proved he didn't need varied landscapes to produce a powerful Western. With just a morally compromised frontier town, Eastwood managed to further define the revisionist ethos that dominated Westerns of the 1970s, intentionally subverting the genre and upsetting old hands like the Duke in the process. Its status as one of the great Westerns of the 1970s has only grown, and rightly so.

Quentin Tarantino took a big gamble making "The Hateful Eight," mainly because he shot it in inclement and unpredictable weather. But it was also somewhat of a gamble because it took place almost entirely in a small cabin and was nothing like Tarantino's previous Western, 2012's "Django Unchained."

The film focuses on eight strangers as they shelter from a blizzard in Minnie's Haberdashery, a stagecoach stopover in Wyoming. These aren't the societal archetypes who found themselves in similarly close quarters back in John Ford's "Stagecoach," however. This wretched octet comprises some of the nastiest individuals to ever roam the Old West. Unsurprisingly, trapping them in a small space for a couple hours results in a series of extremely selfish and violent acts.

"The Hateful Eight" doesn't always appear near the top of Tarantino film rankings. But the movie was never going to be bad considering its cast. Alongside frequent Tarantino collaborators and all-round Hollywood legends Samuel L. Jackson, Kurt Russell, Tim Roth, and Michael Madsen, the ensemble included Jennifer Jason Leigh, Walton Goggins, Demián Bichir, and Western veteran Bruce Dern — the man who shot down John Wayne himself back '72. What's more, "The Hateful Eight" earned three Academy Award nominations: Best Supporting Actress (Jennifer Jason Leigh), Best Cinematography, and Best Original Score, with legendary composer Ennio Morricone winning in the latter category. As such, "The Hateful Eight" is easily one of the best Westerns set in one location, and the only entry on this list to play out mostly in one small room.

Directed by the great John Ford, who knew all too well the value of grouping characters together in a single space following his 1939 triumph "Stagecoach," "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" saw John Wayne and James Stewart collaborate on-screen for the first time. That alone ensured the film would fare well with audiences. But this now legendary Western was about more than the confluence of two major Hollywood careers.

It's significant that the town Shinbone — in which the film plays out — exists in an unnamed state. The town represents the frontier, which in the present day timeline of "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" has been transformed from a lawless land to a more civilized society. But as we discover near the end of the film, that transformation and the success of Stewart's Senator Ransom Stoddard has been built on a lie. Meanwhile, John Wayne's rancher Tom Doniphon is shown to have passed away at the very beginning, establishing a mournful, reflective tone to the film before it flashes back to tell its story of an outlaw felled by Doniphon's bullet and the man who took the credit. Ford appeared to be crafting a sober requiem for the Old West as he'd depicted it throughout his career, for which Shinbone and Wayne stood as symbols.

Interestingly enough, "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" was literally restricted location-wise, having been shot mostly on Paramount sound stages. That coupled with Ford's decision to film in black and white makes the feature feel confined in a way that serves to highlight the human drama and emphasize the sense of the frontier age coming to a close. Shame Ford otherwise made "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" miserable for everyone involved, though.

A revisionist Western everybody should watch at least once, "High Noon" tells the story of Gary Cooper's Marshal Will Kane, who's preparing to leave the frontier town of Hadleyville, New Mexico, with his new bride, Amy (Grace Kelly). When he learns that his former nemesis Frank Miller is on the loose and is headed for Hadleyville, Kane decides to stay and prepare for a confrontation. But this is not your typical Western hero. In fact, rather than facing down his outlaw enemies with the steely resolve of a classic Western gunfighter, he spends most of "High Noon" asking people for help. No such help is forthcoming, and Kane is forced into the final confrontation alone.

Howard Hawks and John Wayne made "Rio Bravo" out of hatred for "High Noon," perhaps predictably given the Duke would never dream of playing a man who gave the impression he needed help of any sort. But the film is considered one of the great Westerns — and all it took was one small town to create a masterpiece of tension and psychological drama.

More importantly, in director Fred Zinnemann's estimation, the town itself was crucial to the story being told. As he put it in his biography, "A Life in the Movies," (via Turner Classic Movies), "[Kane's] town – symbol of a democracy gone soft – faces a horrendous threat to its people's way of life." "High Noon" was about apathy and the loss of a collective belief in standing up for what's right. Like in so many Westerns before and after, then, the town at the center of "High Noon" functioned as a microcosm of society as a whole, and was all Zinnemann and co. needed to tell their story.

Don Siegel's "The Shootist" bowed in 1976, at a time when the era of John Wayne was coming to a close in more ways than one. In a literal sense, the Duke only lasted three more years after the release of this film before he passed away from stomach cancer. In a figurative sense, the traditional big screen Western epitomized by Wayne was, at best, fading. More accurately, it had already been superseded by the revisionist Westerns of directors such as Sam Peckinpah and the man whom Wayne never liked to admit represented his successor, Clint Eastwood.

This story of an aging gunfighter learning he has terminal cancer plays out entirely in Carson City, Nevada. Here, Wayne's John Bernard "J. B." Books arrives and rents a room with Lauren Bacall's Bond Rogers and her son, Gillom Rogers (Ron Howard). Not wanting to die a slow, painful death as a result of his disease, Books arranges to meet three dangerous crack shots at a saloon, and is ultimately felled by a bartender's bullet. The final scene sees Gillom Rogers return the favor, shooting the bartender before tossing Books' gun and seemingly rejecting the notion of following in the footsteps of Wayne's shootist.

This entire story takes place within Carson City, where Books decides to spend his final days as both he and the Old West itself fade. "The Shootist" was Wayne's final film, and while many surely wished he went out with some sort of grandiose ode to both the country that birthed the Western and the genre that made him a star, this comparatively modest swan song, contained within the confines of Carson City, proved to be the perfect farewell.

Bobby Flay definitely hasn't left The Food Network, as he’s got plenty of competition shows to host amid the 2026 TV schedule. But, outside of cooking up a storm, he has also cooked up some sweet love with American chef and restaurateur Brooke Williamson. However, he didn’t do it alone. Flay recently credited actress Scarlett Johansson with his meet-cute romance, and I definitely wasn't expecting to get these details.

While Flay and Williamson interviewed with People, he spoke about hanging out with a friend who helped set him up with his romantic partner. Without name-dropping, he gave some hints like this friend being a huge movie star and being married to SNL’s Colin Jost. Of course, that latter detail was a dead giveaway regarding Johansson!

Flay apparently first met Williamson when they were both judges of Supermarket Stakeout back in 2020. However, he didn’t get together with the Top Chef winner until season 6 of BBQ Brawl five years later. Here’s his true tale of why it took him so long to ask Williamson out and how Johansson helped pick up the pace:

And I was just telling [Johansson] this quandary I was having that I was, like, totally falling for somebody that I work with. And I’m just frustrated because I’m not gonna go there. And I just don’t know what to do. And she told me I was out of my mind. That’s how I sort of came to terms with it. And literally on the very last day of that season of BBQ Brawl, I went up to [Williamson] and I was like, ‘I need to talk to you about something.’ And she’s like, ‘What?’ And I was like, ‘If you’re still interested…’ It had gone on for a while. ‘If you’re still interested, I’m ready to make a commitment to you.’ And that was sort of the beginning of the beginning. There was nothing but support and thrilled that we had decided to make it an actual thing.

Aww, that is too cute for words! It’s adorable that, for a man who knows how to put two and two together when cooking up a delicious dish, he had trouble putting himself together with his beautiful co-worker. I also can't help but love Johansson’s honesty in telling her friend to make a move. The actress may have only played Black Widow in the Marvel movies, but she was a real hero for Flay. And now, Flay and Williamson have been together for over a year.

Before Brooke Williamson, Flay was married three times, so he's certainly had his share of experience with relationships. With that in mind, Flay went on to explain to People what he wanted in a new romance and how that all aligned with Williamson:

I mean, to me, the most important thing is I want a life partner that I’m committed to. I don’t need all of the documentation. But at the same time, I need to make sure that Brooke feels like she’s committed to. We were in London and we were sitting on a bench in The Regent’s Park, and I was like, ‘I got you a gift.’ And I said, ‘But before I give you the gift, like, you’re cool with not getting married, right? Like, we’re on the same page?’ Because we had obviously talked about that. And she’s like, ‘Yeah, yeah, absolutely.’ I was like, ‘Okay.’

So Flay surprised his partner with a huge diamond ring that cemented his commitment to her without a wedding of sorts. To some, it may seem confusing to give the woman you love a ring without the promise of marriage. However, I find it pretty cute, as it’s like a promise ring that still pledges loyalty. And, of course, at the end of the day, it's Flay and Williamson's business as to what they want their relationship to be.

On that note, Bobby Flay and Brooke Williamson seem to be quite happy, and I love to see it. Also, kudos to Scarlett Johansson for intervening a playing a bit of cupid. Fans can watch Flay and Williamson’s Food Network shows using a Hulu subscription or an HBO Max subscription.

#3604. 5 Best Sci-Fi Movies Of 1995, Ranked

1995 was a big year for movies. "Toy Story" launched one of cinema's most reliable hit-makers in Pixar and helped redefine what animation could be. One of the greatest crime thrillers of all time came our way with "Seven." Michael Mann's crowning achievement "Heat" was gifted to action lovers around the world. Nicolas Cage delivered his Oscar-winning performance in "Leaving Las Vegas." But it was also one heck of a year for science fiction.

In terms of historical context, Steven Spielberg's "Jurassic Park" revolutionized Hollywood just two years earlier with its blend of CGI and practical effects, with the industry rapidly adopting computer generated visuals (not always with great results). Meanwhile, other movies were still relying heavily on practical effects, which gives movies from this era a specific feeling. It was a unique time for science fiction, a genre that's often been at the forefront of adoption for new technology in cinema while serving as a breeding ground for underrated gems.

We're going to take a look at the best of the best that sci-fi had to offer viewers in 1995. From groundbreaking anime to rubber suit monster movie goodness and everything in between, there's a little something for everyone here. Let's dig in.

I can't sit here and rightfully say that "Species" is A-class cinema. I can't say that it's the best that the science fiction genre had to offer in the year of our lord 1995. What I can say is that, more than 30 years removed, it's a delightful relic of its time, one that is sexy, ridiculous, and a great deal of fun. Sci-fi doesn't always have to be serious to be seriously enjoyable.

Directed by Roger Donaldson, the film centers on Xavier Fitch (Ben Kingsley) who intercepts a space transmission containing the genetic sequence for an alien life form. He uses it to produce "Sil" (Natasha Henstridge), a gorgeous alien-human hybrid. Fitch's team is concerned by her rapid rate of growth before Sil destroys the laboratory and begins a violent quest for a male human to impregnate her. The U.S. government dispatches top assassin Preston Lennox (Michael Madsen) and a team of experts to stop her.

"Species" is a wacky movie that features some incredible makeup effects and not-so-great CGI. It has Oscar-caliber actors like Sir. Ben Kingsley giving his best to a bonkers script, while guys like Michael Madsen gladly ham it up. It was also a breakout role for the movie's lead, Natasha Henstridge, who has a true scene-stealing presence about her. She is undoubtedly the main reason why this movie sticks out in so many people's minds all these years later.

This also spawned a franchise, with the "Species" sequels bringing DND and T&A to the DTV market. I can't in good conscience recommend those midnight movie sequels to the masses, but I can easily defend the original as a worthwhile bit of '90s sci-fi goodness. (Ryan Scott)

The "Gamera" movies are many things. The original entries are campier kaiju classics oft-remembered as corny fuel for some of the best episodes of "Mystery Science Theater 3000." But the franchise has also produced some genuinely excellent entries in the genre. Case in point: "Gamera: Guardian of the Universe." Directed by Shūsuke Kaneko, this launched a whole new era for the classic Japanese monster, with this particular entry serving as an excellent launching pad for Gamera's grand return.

In this "Gamera" cinematic adventure, a ship runs aground on a mysterious atoll leading to an investigation by insurance representative Kusanagi (Akira Onodera). He discovers an ancient bead that he gives to his daughter Asagi (Ayako Fujitani). Meanwhile, ornithologist Nagamine (Shinobu Nakayama) investigates reports of a new species of large bird named Gyaos. As the Gyaos begin to attack, an ancient guardian with a bond to Asagi emerges.

By the mid-'90s, so much of Hollywood was already relying heavily on CGI to create special effects. Part of what's great about "Guardian of the Universe" is that it still has that tangible, rubber suit monster magic. Yet, technology had gotten better since the '60s and '70s, allowing for those practical effects to shine even brighter. The result? Some of the best practical kaiju action one could ever hope to find.

This film redefined what a "Gamera" movie could be. No longer was this just the lesser-than, turtle-like cousin to "Godzilla." Gamera was undeniably cool now. As was Gyaos, an impeccably designed addition to the franchise. It also served as a springboard for several sequels, including "Gamera 3: Revenge of Iris," one of the best sci-fi movies of 1999. It was a damn fine time for monster movies. (Ryan Scott)

There are dozens of "Godzilla" movies of varying quality dating back to 1954 when the King of the Monsters first debuted on the big screen. But for those who have a fondness for a time when the one they call Gojira was still a rubber suited monster duking it out with other monsters made of rubber, it's hard to do better than "Godzilla vs. Destroyah." Directed by Takao Okawara, it's one of the best "Godzilla" movies of all time.

The film wastes no time as it opens with a burning Godzilla, on the verge of meltdown that could threaten all of humanity, emerging to lay siege to Hong Kong. Meanwhile, horrifying new organisms are discovered in Japan and these crustacean-like creatures are seemingly born of the Oxygen Destroyer, the weapon that killed the original Godzilla. These separate monster problems ultimately lead us to a kaiju clash for the ages.

This is the final entry in the so-called Heisi era of the "Godzilla" franchise, which has by far the best practical monsters in the 70-plus year history of the series. One would be hard-pressed to find more impressive monster designs than that of Destroyah, a hulking, terrifying, hellish vision that is worth the price of admission alone. Plus, the design of the burning Godzilla is unique and metal AF.

With lots of sci-fi craziness, just enough cheese, and some of the best practical kaiju action ever put on the silver screen, this is a must-see for monster movie lovers. Not for nothing, it's the only "Godzilla" movie that currently boasts a perfect critic score on Rotten Tomatoes. It deserves it, in my humble opinion. (Ryan Scott)

A time-travel movie, a post-apocalyptic movie, and all-around a mind-melting piece of sci-fi, "12 Monkeys" is a wild ride. Arguably Terry Gilliam's best film, it loosely adapts Chris Marker's 1962 experimental short film "La Jetée," and follows Bruce Willis as James Cole, a convict sent back in time to find out information about a man-made virus that wiped out most of humanity back in his time. What starts as a relatively simple mission devolves into an exploration of madness, time, and dreams, set in a world that is slowly coming apart. Though made in 1995, the film's focus on how we perceive information and decipher the truth among all the noise is as relevant today as it's ever been. This is not a feel-good movie, but rather a story of rebellion and resilience in a world that tries to tear you apart for perceiving things differently, and Gilliam adequately captures that thought with a cold and dark film that reflects the slow descent into madness of its protagonist.

Even if there's little hope to be found by the end of the movie, "12 Monkeys" is still thrilling and hugely entertaining. It walks the line between commerciality and art, with Gilliam employing two of the biggest stars in Hollywood at the time (Willis and Brad Pitt), while also presenting them without an ounce of vanity. It's a big production, but it sneaks in a provocative and idiosyncratic story with a bleak vision of the future. It also has a layered story that never compromises its singular vision. (Rafael Motamayor)

There are few sci-fi films as generation-defining as Mamoru Oshii's adaptation of Masamune Shirow's "Ghost in the Shell." This is a film that's inspired countless filmmakers around the globe, in both animation and live-action. We wouldn't have "The Matrix" if it wasn't for "Ghost in the Shell," and titans like James Cameron and Steven Spielberg count themselves among its many fans. Plus, it's just genuinely a thrilling and monumental piece of science-fiction cinema. The film is set in the then-distant future, at a time when most people have some sort of cybernetic implant and some even have cyber brains that allow access to the internet. The story follows a cyborg public security agent hunting down an enigmatic hacker.

Mamoru Oshii does a great job of condensing the complex and dense plotting of the original manga, while adding his own take on the material. This is a dark film with austere seriousness that meditates on the nature of self, identity, and our relationship with technology. It can take several viewings to fully grasp the many thematic layers present in this film and the way each scene builds on some thematic idea, adding to the main character's crisis of identity as she contemplates how much of her humanity is left under all her cybernetic implants. "Ghost in the Shell" is also a straight-up beautiful movie to look at, with Production I.G delivering a stunning combination of traditional cel animation with CGI animation. In many ways, this is the '90s answer to "Akira" in how the film pushes forward what animation can do, with lens effects and attention to light and shadow serving to make a film that looks like nothing before or since. (Rafael Motamayor)

#3603. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3602. The No. 1 Horror Movie of 2026 Is Officially Leaving Peacock

Unless you have a One Wish Willow, you'll want to get your final watch in

Not many directors can say their debut film was a blockbuster hit, let alone a cultural phenomenon. But newcomer Curry Barker, who wrote and directed Obsession, the No. 1 horror movie of 2026, can say he's accomplished both. The film takes a look at the dangers of getting exactly what you wish for when Bear (Michael Johnston) makes a wish that his friend Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette) would love him more than anyone else in the world. Despite being made on only a $750,000 budget, the film dominated the box office when it hit theaters, earning $17.2 million in its first week and a staggering $23.9 million in its second week.

To date, Obsession remains the tenth most profitable film of 2026 at the worldwide box office according to data from Box Office Mojo, earning a gross total of $523 million during its theatrical run. It's no surprise that when Obsession moved to streaming, it continued finding success on Peacock, but going into November, the end of Obsession's victory lap is officially drawing near.

Obsession is leaving Peacock on Nov. 17, 2026, the same date that the film is expected to launch on Netflix in the United States. The film first hit Peacock on July 17, 2026, and drew in 456 million minutes streamed in just its first two days on the service, according to data from Nielsen. It went on to spend more than 150 days on JustWatch’s U.S. streaming Top 10 list, further cementing its domination in the industry.

Obsession was more than just a blockbuster and streaming hit. It became a cultural phenomenon in the months that followed its release, with fans drawn into conversations online about the film's themes surrounding bodily autonomy and consent. A Nikki Freeman actor drew thousands of visitors to California's Halloween Horror Nights this fall, including Inde Navarette herself, and Obsession reached as far as Fortnite, where a Nikki Freeman skin was released for the game in November 2026 (complete with a "No, No, No..." emote).

Even Barker, who first built a following for himself making sketches and short films on YouTube, didn't expect the success that came with Obsession. In a June 2026 interview with the Associated Press, he said, "“That’s when you start to feel this impostor syndrome of like: What? It’s not that good. All I see when I watch ‘Obsession’ is the problems.”

The film follows Bear (Michael Johnston), a lonely, awkward man with strong, unrequited feelings for his friend Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette). After failing to confess his feelings, Bear stumbles upon a One Wish Willow in a novelty shop. The instructions seem simple enough: make a wish, break the willow stick, and watch your deepest desires come true, but when Bear wishes for Nikki to love him more than anyone else in the entire world, his dream quickly turns into a nightmare. The film has received plenty of praise from critics and audience members, including Polygon writer Jesse Hassenger, who wrote, "Navarrette gets plenty of time to believably and charmingly establish who Nikki is before the wish takes her true self away. Once that happens, she does bravura work as this imitation version, regularly flying off the handle with panicked eagerness or cackling mania, creating an unusual combination of fear and pity — a true movie monster crossing possession with a Bride of Frankenstein figure."

It's worth noting that Obsession's move to Netflix this month comes as awards season nears, and it could very well be a strategic decision to keep the film in the spotlight. Focus Features, the production company behind Obsession, is definitely pushing for consideration in the forthcoming Academy Awards. The company's website suggests Obsession for Best Picture, Inde Navarrette for Best Actress, and Curry Barker for Best Original Screenplay, among other categories.

Obsession is about to get another boom in viewership

#3601. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

#3600. The Best King Ghidorah Movie To Watch After Godzilla Minus Zero Is Streaming On HBO Max

"Godzilla Minus Zero" may not be as good as its immediate predecessor, but Takashi Yamazaki brings some truly spectacular kaiju action to the big screen in his "Godzilla Minus One" sequel. The film has a sense of scope and scale that we haven't really seen in the 70-year-old franchise, with impeccable VFX that capture the sheer destruction of the giant monsters that battle it out in the movie. Yamazaki also captures the true horrors of what a kaiju attack would look like, putting the film's R-rating to good use with some gruesome imagery.

The highlight of the movie is, surprisingly enough, not Godzilla. Instead, it's the golden, armless dragon with three heads and two tails known as Ghidorah. "Godzilla Minus Zero" retains Ghidorah's alien origin while reimagining him as a translucent blob that absorbs creatures and adopts their traits, allowing him to evolve into a three-headed dragon that shoots lightning and can make things float.

Though Ghidorah's design unfortunately leaked before the film's release, he still looks absolutely perfect. More so, the character brings some silliness to Yamazaki's take on the Godzilla universe, as the inclusion of aliens means future sequels can now bring in anything from Mechagodzilla to even Gigan. And yet, Ghidorah remains scary and awe-inspiring. It's easy to see why he's been Godzilla's main archenemy for decades and is the one kaiju that, at least in the eyes of the public, presents a real threat to the king of the monsters.

Unfortunately, despite him showing up in over a dozen movies, most of Ghidorah's film appearances aren't that great. Luckily, the best Ghidorah movie, by far, is currently streaming on HBO Max — namely, the king of terror's debut in the appropriately titled 1964 film "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster."

"Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" was released back in 1964 as the fifth film in the Godzilla franchise, bringing together Godzilla, Mothra, and Rodan, who must all team up to take down the titular Ghidorah (lest the kaiju cause humanity to perish).

This is not only one of the best Godzilla movies of all time, it's also a hugely important film in the long-running franchise. That's because the movie marked a change in the king of monsters, introducing the idea of Godzilla as humankind's savior rather than just a destructive force. Up until that point, Godzilla would either attack human cities or battle other kaiju, but the latter scenario tended to center around some kind of territorial dispute or petty grievance. In other words, Godzilla would act more like a grumpy old man trying to keep kids off his lawn than a hero.

"Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster," however, fully transformed Godzilla into a force for good that would team up with other monsters in an effort to defend the people of Earth. Indeed, for decades after that, the king of the monsters would mostly help defend humans against other threats, taking on the likes of MechaGodzilla, Biollante, and plenty of other kaijus.

On top of that, "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" is just plain fun as a movie. Director Ishirō Honda finds a great balance between the serious tone of his original 1954 "Godzilla" (which focuses on the horror that surrounds the kaiju) and the campiness that would become a staple of the "Godzilla" franchise in the coming years. It's a rather ambitious film, too, with four monsters sharing the screen, yet it never feels too busy or disjointed.

Though Godzilla has fought plenty of villains over the last 70 years, none have managed to leave a lasting impact the way King Ghidorah has. When he was first introduced, kaiju were either all bad or portrayed as animals we should root against. But Ghidorah was the first proper villain of the "Godzilla" franchise, and he is treated as such. "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" takes its time teasing the arrival of the titular dragon, building dread and making sure you understand Ghidorah is a big enough threat that Godzilla would actually join forces with other kaiju to take him down.

It's why 2019's rather underrated "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" borrows so much from "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster," pairing Godzilla with the same allies he has in the 1964 film in order to square off with the more powerful Ghidorah. That movie understands that a three-headed dragon that shoots lightning is already a pretty imposing image and the perfect way to make Godzilla appear heroic.

Now, "Godzilla Minus Zero" has continued that tradition, turning King Ghidorah into a terrifying monster. This new movie isn't in a hurry to bring Godzilla back, and in the meantime, we watch as Ghidorah lays waste to Japan, causing harrowing devastation with his terrific powers (including the ability to make buildings levitate, which he uses to kill a whole bunch of people by dropping them to their painful deaths). The film also introduces the idea of Ghidorah constantly evolving, with his design changing throughout the movie as he grows heads, turns golden, and ultimately gains Godzilla-like dorsal plates, along with the king of the monsters' ability to wield atomic breath.

Ghidorah will always be Godzilla's greatest foe, and you can watch his first and best appearance on HBO Max.

One thing I love about book-to-screen adaptations of classics like The Cat In The Hat is how each new iteration reimagines a character we already love. Bill Hader’s version comes over two decades after the Mike Myers movie, and one peculiar new thing I noticed about his animated take on the character is the fact that he has a flip phone. Random, right?

When CinemaBlend spoke to Hader about his latest role, I had to ask about the little detail I noticed about his The Cat In The Hat. Here’s how the SNL alum responded:

Because Cat in the Hat's real. Cat in the Hat doesn't need to fit in with whatever's happening now, you know?

For some reason, it just feels right that The Cat would have a flip phone (and one that even has a crystal-clear video chat function). Plus, this detail about The Cat definitely adds to his unique character in a cute way, as it's revealed in the film that he’s been doing house calls to bring play into the lives of kids for multiple generations. So, perhaps the flip phone tells us that he's a bit old school. Bill Hader also said this about the topic:

I think it was funny that it was a flip phone. I have friends who have flip phones, and they remember things better than me. They are not as distracted as me. They seem much happier than me.

Hey, maybe The Cat is onto something. I mean the character is all about bringing playtime and wonder to kids. Why would he need a smartphone for that?

These days, a lot more people are ditching their smartphones for more primitive technology like flip phones to get away from things like social media addiction. Chris Pine, for example, had one for four years before switching to the latest technology and finding himself wanting to “immediately go back”. Other famous people known to have a flip phone are Christopher Nolan, Anna Wintour and Rihanna – so The Cat can count himself among icons.

A lot of other Y2K trends have been coming back lately, too. For example, both Kylie Jenner and Ariana Grande recently admitted their love for wired earphones (and I’m totally with them). I’ve seen a lot of younger people out with their digital cameras at concerts too. When you think about it, The Cat In The Hat’s “dumb phone” is very in with the kids.

There’s already The Cat In The Hat trend; maybe this could be part of a new wave of less phone dependence and more focus on fun and creativity, like the character itself has been teaching kids since the picture book came out back in 1957.

You can check out the new The Cat In The Hat movie in theaters now.
