#3547. How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying

No one is doing monster movies quite like director Takashi Yamazaki and his team — who not once but twice now, with “Godzilla Minus One” and “Godzilla Minus Zero,” have made Godzilla feel both bigger than Tokyo Bay and extremely emotional and personal, even handcrafted. Much of that comes down to the narrative balance between our human heroes and the King of the Monsters, of course. But it’s also about the grounded, physical ways the monsters are brought to life.

Much has already been made of the fact that both Godzilla’s and King Ghidorah’s roars were recorded by blasting the sound effects against real physical spaces (and probably scaring some hikers in the process) so we wouldn’t just hear something otherworldly. We’d hear the texture of the loudspeakers, the reverberation of the sound on the concrete of a dam (for Ghidorah) or a dome (for Godzilla) — the unreal brought into a real, physical space. Related Stories ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

But that is only the light-up blue tip of the kaiju for the work done by the “Godzilla Minus Zero” sound design team. Sound designer Natsuko Inoue and production and post-production sound mixer Hisafumi Takeuchi constantly found ways to tie the most fantastical moments back to Earth, because that sonic believability keeps the audience invested in the action.

“ When audiences hear sounds that they’ve never heard before too frequently, I think it removes you from the world because it’s too foreign and it’ll stand out,” Inoue told IndieWire. “Once a fantasy-like or fictitious sound goes through the sort of real-world echo, then it becomes a lot more palatable, or we become more receptive to how it sounds because it’s echoing in a way that we recognize. So that was a way that we really tied the visuals to the sound and made it feel more grounded.”

This grounding process is especially important, and especially challenging, when things that should be on the ground take to the air as a part of Ghidorah’s gravity beam. Inoue did an initial pass of the sound effect for the beam that allows Ghidorah to throw whole houses up in the air high enough for our favorite eternally tormented, former Kamikaze pilot Kôichi Skikishima (Ryûnosuke Kamiki) to fly past them. But it wasn’t quite right.

“So I went back into the Foley studio, and I wanted to capture that feeling of something being lifted and rising. I took this very small speaker, and I placed it right next to a bunch of different objects — a sheet of metal or some wood or a water tank — to capture a sound that almost felt distorted,” Inoue said.

That distortion, bounced off different types of objects, captured the sensation Inoue was after: the sonic equivalent of your stomach lifting into your mouth.

“Oftentimes in sound design, when you layer too many sounds or put too much processing on it, it starts to ruin the original material or the original sound that you’ve captured. So this distortion became a very strong foundation. I didn’t add too much post-processing on it,” Inoue said.

What she did do was hand it over to Takeuchi to create the sense of whole blocks caught up in Ghidorah’s gravity beam and preserve the dialogue and add background dialogue, so that we’re always afraid for the human beings in danger during Ghidorah’s rampages.

When Shikishima first flies through Ghidorah’s gravity beam, the sound team really wanted to lean into the character’s emotional response to something that’s mindbendingly horrible. “I added a Doppler effect — so like when an ambulance or a police car drives by and the sound shifts slightly — [to give] the sensation that you’re passing through,” Takeuchi told IndieWire.

It’s that shifting of sound, more than any one particular sound, that adds a scale to the horror beyond what Shikishima or what we can see. “We wanted to be very mindful of the balance and what it was doing and what it was supposed to do for each scene,” Takeuchi said.

“What we were trying to do is take sounds that you would hear in nature and then design and add to it in almost like an extension type of way, and that’s how we make the Kaiju as well as the gravity beam feel more real,” Inoue added.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now playing in theaters.

#3546. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. #3545. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3544. Letterboxd’s Sale to the New York Times: 9 Pros, Cons, and Big Questions from the $330 Million Deal

After several months of business talks and speculation, Letterboxd is about to have new owners. The New York Times is closing in on deal to acquire the film-logging social media platform, which values the company at $330 million. It’s an eye-popping increase from 2023, when the Canadian holding company Tiny bought a majority stake at a $50 million valuation.

Far beyond the film industry, there is a dismal track record and daunting uncertainty when it comes to companies’ ability to maintain their identities after being acquired. Social media reception to the pending New York Times deal generally peaked at resigned relief (“the best case scenario” was a common refrain) while also drawing more cynical, even existential responses about the future of Letterboxd. As the website’s user base holds its breath over the future, these are some pros, cons, and big unknowns to consider about where Letterboxd is going. Related Stories Letterboxd Finalizing $330 Million Sale to The New York Times ‘The Weed Eaters’ Lands Expanded Release from Yellow Veil Pictures: New Zealand Cannibal Movie Sets Winter Rollout

There’s understandably a lot of negative social chatter about the news of Letterboxd’s looming acquisition, but let’s rest assured that it’s at least not a studio taking ownership of the wildly popular cinephile engagement platform. A24, Sony, Netflix, and Skydance were all reported to have registered talks about an acquisition. Whether or not this new iteration of Letterboxd will exist behind a paywall is one matter, but that’s not the worst thing compared to the potential studio-ification (i.e. A24-ification, as they were in talks for the sale) of the brand. Compare it to studios running an exhibition chain — not just Sony purchasing Alamo Drafthouse, but all the way back to the days before the Paramount Decrees, which legislatively blocked studios from having a monopoly on theaters. (Decrees that are no longer in effect.) In that situation, there’s more potential for marketing nepotism and favoritism to titles and properties in-house. A media company taking over Letterboxd should, in theory, prevent the kind of self-interest that threatens independence. —Ryan Lattanzio

A deal would bring two unusually loaded cultural conversations under one roof. The movie-logging platform has helped reshape the world’s repertory film scene — effectively gamifying the enjoyment of archival art — while debates about the Times often wind their way back to the paper’s coverage of Palestine and trans rights. For Letterboxd users who see that coverage as having real consequences for whose lives and experiences are taken seriously by mainstream journalistic institutions, the prospect of the Times owning a community they helped build raises questions of trust. A bigger audience would be a genuine upside, but for some users, who owns the room is an existential issue. —Alison Foreman

While some users might not even know about Letterboxd’s digital magazine, the Journal has been a growing presence on the platform, with a staffed editorial team regularly publishing interviews, retrospective considerations, film festival coverage, and other longform articles. The question remains on how, or if, those writers and editors will be integrated into the New York Times newsroom. A shuttering of the Journal would wreck yet another publication for professional film coverage and freelance opportunities, of which there are fewer and fewer. On the other hand, when the New York Times bought The Athletic in 2022 for a whopping $550 million, the banner initially continued as a semi-independent banner. But a year later, the Times dissolved its existing sports department, laying off or reassigning staff, and positioned The Athletic as a replacement. The New York Times’ culture desk has not been immune to shake-ups over recent years; the potential addition of Letterboxd begs the question of whether further changes are in store. —J. Kim Murphy

As the number of Letterboxd accounts has skyrocketed over the past few years, navigating the platform has become a bumpier experience for users. Pop-up Cloudflare turnstiles reading “Verifying you are human. This may take a few seconds” make frequent interruptions clicking from page to page, while Gremlins-centric error messages signaling server crashes are semi-regular occurrences. The New York Times draws much more web traffic than Letterboxd and such technical hiccups are essentially anomalous. The company certainly has the resources to bolster the strength of Letterboxd’s servers. —JKM

Letterboxd users have historically been an extremely discerning audience, sensitive to changes that might be seen as minute or inconsequential for other websites. A memorable hiccup from recent years came when the platform abruptly removed an option to list out all star-ratings given by the accounts one follows on a single web page. After some backlash from users (like myself) who noticed the feature’s disappearance, Letterboxd was swift in reintegrating the tool. It was a small crisis with a happy ending, but it speaks to how quickly UI changes can dishearten the platform’s users. If the New York Times wants to make even small tweaks to the platform, or heavily integrate it into its digital ecosystem, it will face an audience that’s quick to rally against such changes. —JKM

The New York Times Company is the poster child for brand elasticity in the digital media age. America’s newspaper of record didn’t just adapt to the Internet; it built an empire of games, recipes, and sports that a sizable chunk of the world needs to engage with in a daily basis. But it’s less apparent how Letterboxd fits into the strategy. The social network exists somewhere between an editorial product and a game and doesn’t have a clear comp within the NYT organization. Is the plan to simply move the entire Letterboxd infrastructure behind the NYT paywall, making the $30 monthly subscription tier even more unavoidable for cinephiles? Draw on users’ data to bolster revenue opportunities for streaming promotions and the Times’ product recommendation banner Wirecutter? The answer might be some combination of the above, but the Times is entering uncharted territory. —Christian Zilko

Plenty of filmmakers IndieWire has spoken to are concerned about the widening gap between what defines film criticism and what defines a hot-take social media sound-off, i.e., the “instant reaction.” Reviews on Letterboxd can range from the thoughtful and long-form to the pithy and snarky. As film critic jobs evaporate globally, what happens when you merge Letterboxd closer to the purview of established, institutional film writing, the kind that’s hard, that demands a chunk of your soul? Letterboxd has further democratized criticism, no question, and while many of us argue that we need an elevated discourse, what happens if more people start to think… we don’t? Will the fusion of the Times and Letterboxd stoke that debate, or create harmony? Will this only fuel the growing primacy of influencers over critics and journalists as an authority on a film’s quality? Either way, cantankerous conversation will abound. —RL

It follows then that if enough Letterboxd users distrust the Times, they might log fewer movies, post fewer reviews, or exit the app altogether. From a web-development perspective, the basic mechanics of a movie diary are incredibly easy to replicate. (Hell, AI just cloned Adobe Photoshop.) The hard part is getting the consumers whose aggregate taste is a cultural bellwether to once again show up in the same place. It wouldn’t take a mass exodus for Letterboxd to feel fundamentally different, and if the core group of people who reliably made consumers laugh or put weird repertory picks on your radar stop contributing, there will be fewer reasons to engage. The community could splinter across new competitor sites — which, yes, opens up potential opportunities for aspiring critics to gain exposure and find their followings. But we can’t know if any of that would be as big as the OG Letterboxd. —AF

#3543. DC’s Upcoming Green Lantern Release Is Everything The DCU’s Next Project Should Be

DC reveals the first glimpse at Hal Jordan's next battle, which looks like the ideal basis for the DCU's future Green Lantern movie and show appearances. HBO’s Lanterns marks a remarkable milestone as the first live-action, non-cameo Green Lantern project since the critical and commercial stumble of 2011's Green Lantern movie. The fifteen-year drought feels especially strange given how central the Emerald Knights are to the broader DC Universe and the superhero genre as a whole. Yet, for over a decade following Ryan Reynolds’s polarizing outing, the Lanterns were largely relegated to brief, peripheral nods.

Fortunately, this return is only the beginning, as the Green Lanterns are playing a vital role in the expanding DCU. Following the events of the HBO series' first season, both Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart and Nathan Fillion’s Guy Gardner are confirmed to reunite on the big screen in James Gunn’s upcoming sequel Man of Tomorrow. With the two Lanterns joining Superman and Lex Luthor to confront Brainiac, their presence in the 2027 movie pulls them from grounded terrestrial mysteries to world-scale war. New Lantern heroes and their respective villains could be introduced soon afterward, as their lore seems to be developing faster than that of any other DCU character.

Before Man of Tomorrow adds unbridled sci-fi and fantasy to John Stewart's DCU story, DC Comics shows how visually stunning a full-scale Green Lantern movie or show would look.

Hal Jordan’s clash against the returning Green Lantern villain Krona and the Manhunters in Green Lantern Corps showcases the perfect scale and tone missing from the DCU's Lanterns adaptation. In Green Lantern Corps #22, Hal Jordan teams up Krona, Jayna, and Tobi Y2K to dive deep into the wild Nexus of Emotions, where they meet face to face with the Manhunters. The heroes' varied costumes and powers, the Manhunters' colorful yet intimidating appearance, and the incredibly vibrant landscape of the Nexus of Emotions create a breathtaking visual experience that has never been adapted to live-action in a DC movie or show.

Although the HBO series Lanterns presents a bold and interesting take on the Greek Lantern mythos with its gritty crime-thriller murder mystery, the psychedelic visuals of Green Lantern Corps are something no live-action adaptation has dared to try. Now that Lanterns has introduced a new version of the Corps grounded on Earth, John Stewart's return in James Gunn's bombastic Man of Tomorrow and other future DCU Green Lantern appearances should draw inspiration from the comics and provide an unapologetically hard sci-fi story starring one or more Green Lanterns, especially if Nathan Fillion's scenery-chewing Guy Gardner has a key role in the plot.

Despite the immense popularity of the franchise, the Green Lantern Corps have yet to showcase their full cosmic majesty in live-action. On the big screen, the 2011 Green Lantern movie isolated Hal Jordan on a predictable hero's journey that barely scratched the surface of Oa's vast alien lore, Zack Snyder's Justice League only featured Yalan Gur in a single flashback scene, and James Gunn's Superman only included Guy Gardner in a supporting role. The DCU's Lanterns narrowed its scope and focused entirely on Hal Jordan and John Stewart's grounded mystery bound strictly to Earth.

DC is subtly revolutionizing the Green Lantern mythos, paving the way for the Corps to take a more prominent and completely fresh role.

A new Green Lantern big-screen adaptation could showcase multiple Earth Lanterns fighting side by side, complementing each other's constructs in creative team-up maneuvers with their own unique spin on their weapons. Audiences have yet to witness the sheer thrill of large-scale, live-action space warfare where hundreds of diverse ring-slingers engage in chaotic construct-filled battles against iconic Green Lantern villains such as the Sinestro Corps, the Black Lanterns, and the Manhunters. While the DCU presents a very different perspective, there's still room for a large-scale, colorful take on the Lanterns in the big or the small screen.

Which Green Lantern character would you want to see in live-action?

Green Lantern Corps #22 is available November 11 from DC Comics

#3542. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3541. 3 Best 2026 Books To Read Before the Year Ends

We are almost at the end of the year, that magical time when we start to feel like we didn't do nearly enough. So few of us actually get to fulfill our New Year's resolutions — if we have resolutions at all — but there is still time to do a few of them; it's only November, after all. If your resolution was to read a bit more, then you're in luck, because 2026 had a slew of great books, some of which you might not have read yet.

Better late than never, and early November is still a great time for you to pick up one of these 2026 gems and lose yourself in their engaging narratives. Maybe they're a great fantasy adventure, or maybe they're a romantic drama — the point is, these 2026 books are amazing, and you still have time to start and finish them before the ball drops on December 31.

Let's begin with a cute romantasy book, because who doesn't love romantasy? Sea of Charms is the third standalone entry in the Spellshop series and tells a classic high-seas adventure with plenty of romance and fantasy to boot. The plot follows Marin, a supplier runner who journeys from island to island to deliver goods alongside her crew. On the island of Alyssium, Marin meets Dax, a stubborn composer whom she convinces to pose as her boyfriend in the upcoming End-of-Harvest festival.

Sea of Charms blends a typical romcom plot with a thrilling adventure at sea, and the result is one of the most singular and enchanting books of 2026. Every cozy trope that romance fans love is alive and well here: fake dating? Check! Found family? Check! Self-discovery amid hardship? Check! What else can you ask for? Author Sarah Beth Durst's writing is witty, atmospheric, and utterly irresistible, making it impossible not to fall for Marin and Dax. Mainly, her immersive prose will make it impossible to put Sea of Charms down, and at 384 pages, it's a perfect choice to finish before Christmas Day. However, perhaps there's no better time to read this than in the week between Christmas and New Year.

Now for something a lot more serious and relevant. The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State is a non-fiction book about, you guessed it, AI. Written by Harvard historian Jill Lepore, the book deals with heavy issues concerning how artificial intelligence and corporations are messing with the democratic process. Lepore tracks the evolution of systems purportedly designed to help democracy, including ID numbers and consensus techniques, and describes how they have become tools for mass surveillance and categorization.

In a world where AI is such a hot topic of discussion, books like The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State become all the more relevant and important. Interestingly, Lepore tracks how many of sci-fi's most daring ideas, first presented in books and movies, have been developed in real life, ultimately amounting to the situation we find ourselves in right now. The author also pulls no punches when it comes to condemning oligarchs and tech moguls, who keep pushing for invasive technologies aimed at slowly eroding democracy. Non-fiction books can be just as compelling as any work of narrative fiction, and this gem proves it; chances are there is no 2026 book more passionate or urgent than this one.

Finally, we have a wonderfully original book that updates F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby for the new millennium. Last Night in Brooklyn is set in 2007, shortly before the 2008 financial crisis that would shape much of the early 2010s lifestyle. The protagonist is Alicia Canales Forten, a 26-year-old whose conventional life is upended by her mysterious and alluring neighbor, a designer known as La Garza.

A genderbent version of The Great Gatsby might not be particularly interesting in and of itself, but author Xochitl Gonzalez opts for a modern and insightful approach. Here, she deals with classic themes in line with the setting — indeed, everything from economic uncertainty to class and racial struggles can be found here. However, Gonzalez is far more perceptive than the average writer, particularly concerning issues of ambition and what it means to exist in a world driven by appearance and money. Moreover, the book is incredibly atmospheric, with the author painting a vibrant, explosive vision of Brooklyn that feels powerful, irresistibly immersive, and ultimately unforgettable.

#3540. Eric Bauza’s Final ‘Looney Tunes’ Performance Is ‘Daffy Season,’ Now in Theaters Ahead of ‘The Cat in the Hat’

The death of Eric Bauza in October shocked the entertainment industry. An impressively prolific voice actor, it would’ve been nearly impossible for anybody engaging with animation over the past 15 years to never come across his work. Bauza’s death came just two months after the delayed release of “Coyote vs. Acme,” the “Looney Tunes” feature once deemed unreleasable by Warner Bros. Discovery and later sold off to Ketchup Entertainment. The film, which grossed $101 million worldwide, is a true showcase for Bauza, who lends his voice to a plethora of iconic characters, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Tweety, and Porky Pig. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Roars with $6.7 Million in Previews, ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’ Earns $3.5 Million David Ellison’s Big Bet: Why the Mogul Thinks Skydance Film Chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein Can Deliver 30 Movies a Year

Bauza became something of the defining voice of modern “Looney Tunes” in his final years. Fans can see him give one final performance with the property in “Daffy Season,” a 7-minute animated short that plays before screenings of “The Cat in the Hat,” opening Friday from Skydance’s Warner Bros. Pictures. A representative for the studio confirmed to IndieWire that the short is Bauza’s final “Looney Tunes” movie. Bauza is also credited as providing additional voices for “The Cat in the Hat.”

“Daffy Season” centers on Daffy Duck, voiced by Bauza. He’s joined by Jeff Bergman as Bugs Bunny, Gabriel Iglesias as Speedy Gonzales, and Jeannie Tirado as Lola Bunny. The plot follows Daffy, turning his beak up at his fellow Tunes as they mindlessly obsess over the game of soccer. Todd Wilderman and Hamish Grieve are co-directors. “Daffy Season” is the first theatrically released “Looney Tunes” short since “Daffy’s Rhapsody” played before “Journey 2: The Mysterious Island” back in 2012.

Before “Daffy Season,” Bauza had already provided some voice work for a “Tunes” musical feature titled “Bye Bye Bunny,” which was canceled after some years of development and production. Other “Looney Tunes” credits from Bauza include the HBO Max series “Looney Tunes Cartoons” and the features “The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie” and “Space Jam: A New Legacy.”

Bauza died at his home in Los Angeles on October 25 as a result of hypertensive cardiovascular disease. In a tribute in The Hollywood Reporter, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation producer Susan Rogers credited Bauza with playing a huge role in reviving the “Looney Tunes.”

“There wasn’t a single short he couldn’t quote or couldn’t reference,” she said. “I don’t think you replace Eric Bauza … The hole he leaves is huge. There are many talented people out there, and the franchise will move on. But there’s only one Eric Bauza.”

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. #3537. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3536. 10 Best YA Fantasy Books Of All Time

Many of the most successful books of the last few decades have been YA fantasy novels. From supernatural romances to grand magical adventures, young readers have fallen so head-over-heels in love with the fictional worlds they never wanted to leave that the genre is one of the strongest in modern literature. What’s more, their appeal extends well beyond teenagers. The excitement of a solid literary fantasy adventure is entertaining no matter one's age, even if the commercially-targeted readership is explicitly young adults.

Countless novels will always be considered classics of the genre, but the best YA fantasy books stand apart, and their status is hard to argue against. Many have transcended their original readership to become the foundations of iconic pop culture properties. Whether they send readers to faerie courts, supernatural criminal underworlds, dystopian versions of earth, or hidden magic schools, the greatest YA fantasy novels account for some of the most exciting and emotionally engaging stories modern literature has to offer.

Few YA fantasy books understand the all-consuming intensity of first love as effectively as Twilight. Stephenie Meyer makes the supernatural romance between sparkling vampire Edward and new girl in town Bella feel more magical and awe-inspiring than any of the story’s supernatural elements. The intensity and directness of the couple’s romantic journey means readers are invested long before the deeper lore and fantasy worldbuilding fully take shape.

The four original Twilight novels also tap into common young-adult anxieties around belonging. The supernatural families are used to explore questions about loyalty and independence, giving Bella’s romantic choices consequences beyond simply choosing a partner. While there are certain elements of the later plot that became divisive, such as the idea of werewolf imprinting, the way Stephenie Meyer gives Bella’s uncertainty and longing as much of a presence as the series’ supernatural elements ensures it will always be a YA fantasy staple.

You can purchase Twilight, the first novel in the Twilight series by Stephenie Meyer, here.

Faerie courts are common territory in YA fantasy, but they rarely feel as hostile or full of danger like in Holly Black's The Folk of the Air novels. Beginning with 2018’s The Cruel Prince, the trilogy treats etiquette, bargains, and social standing as practical instruments of power just as important as any sword or spell. The central heroine of the series, Jude, is a mortal girl raised in this dangerous faerie world after her parents’ murder. Jude has ambitions beyond mere survival, and it’s here that The Folk of the Air novels gain their brilliance as reading experiences beyond their fantasy setting.

Unlike many YA fantasy heroes, Jude is openly aggressive and confrontational, and Holly Black’s willingness to embrace such an abrasive protagonist immediately distinguishes The Folk of the Air novels. Jude’s victory isn’t based on any kind of divine destiny. She’s not a humble ordinary person who finds themselves suddenly imbued with great power. Her success requires an open appetite for manipulation and seeing one’s foes defeated, a rarity among central YA fantasy characters. Anyone who enjoys worlds where a backhanded compliment is just as dangerous as a concealed dagger will find The Folk of the Air books among the most satisfying that YA fantasy has to offer.

You can purchase The Cruel Prince, the first novel in The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black, here.

Any decent heist story requires a memorable ensemble group of characters, especially when it blends with other genres. Leigh Bardugo completely understands this with her Six of Crows duology, which is part of the author’s Grishaverse universe. Bardugo uses the heist story structure to embark on an incredibly satisfying character-focused adventure, with the elaborate schemes of Kaz Brekker and his five talented specialists almost taking a secondary focus to the intense interpersonal drama between the crew’s members.

It’s incredibly impressive how emotional material weaves so seamlessly with criminal adventure, and this is why Six of Crows and its sequel, Crooked Kingdom, count among the best YA fantasy novels (and are definitely the best Grishaverse stories). Relationships and trust only develop through intense patience, testing and setting of boundaries, and difficult choices, which gives enormous weight to every new friendship or unexpected portrayal. Combined with the commercial brutality of the setting Ketterdam, this character-first approach leads to a YA fantasy crime story whose brilliance extends far beyond its twists.

You can purchase Six of Crows, the first novel in the Six of Crows duology by Leigh Bardugo, here.

The Harry Potter books make magical education feel like an experience readers have personally shared. Lessons, examinations, rivalries, meals, and school holidays make Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry one of the most satisfying settings in any YA fantasy series. Across the seven Harry Potter novels, the Wizarding World becomes as fleshed out as any of the book’s characters. This leads to the central conflict over its fate between Harry and Voldemort feeling far more consequential and important than almost any other fictional battle between good and evil.

What’s more, while the worldbuilding of the Harry Potter books accounts for why they remain so beloved after decades, the story itself taps into many of the themes that define the best YA fantasy. The friendship between Harry, Ron, and Hermione remains the emotional foundation throughout, and this keeps the ever-expanding mythology grounded and ensures every victory and defeat resonates with readers. Few fantasy series balance the satisfaction of an individual school-year adventure with the momentum of a larger conflict quite so successfully.

You can purchase Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone, the first novel in the Harry Potter series by J.K. Rowling, here.

Lyrical prose can give literary fantasy tremendous atmosphere, and Daughter of Smoke & Bone brings this appeal to the YA corner of the genre. Author Laini Taylor’s imagery gives every setting, character, and creature a vivid physical presence, making the extraordinary feel real enough to touch. The opening novel introduces readers to Karou, a 17-year-old art student whose mysterious errands connect everyday Prague to a much stranger hidden world. The many twists, turns, and shock revelations give the story a lot of momentum, but it’s Taylor’s writing style that elevates the three Daughter Of Smoke & Bone novels from simply being great YA fantasy stories to among the greatest books in the genre.

There’s a lot of deep thematic work in the Daughter Of Smoke & Bone books too, especially when it comes to exploring which side is truly good and which is truly evil in a seemingly traditional fantasy conflict. Ideas like romance, grief, and vengeance also complicate matters and add a distinct spin to Karou’s journey and place in the wider battle between the angelic Seraphim and human-animal hybrid Chimaera. The result is a philosophically rich reading experience whose emotional depth is supported by some truly beautiful prose. Throw in a great magic system and a perfect tonal balance between its fantasy and romance and this secures itself as an essential reading for YA fantasy fan.

You can purchase Daughter of Smoke & Bone, the first novel in the Daughter of Smoke & Bone trilogy by Laini Taylor, here.

Rebellion forms the center of many YA fantasy narratives, but few examine how oppression is actually enforced quite like Sabaa Tahir’s An Ember in the Ashes quartet. Violence in Tahir’s Roman-inspired world is reinforced through education, punishment, status, and the constant narrowing of available choices, which the author explores with chilling detail. The plot places readers on both sides of the oppressor-oppressed divide, with the story split between scholar Laia’s attempts to rescue her imprisoned brother from the regime, and soldier Elias’s questioning of the social structure he helps to violently enforce.

The alternating viewpoints of Laia and Elias become an incredibly effective lens through which the An Ember in the Ashes novels explore the relationship between freedom and rebellion. The world of the Martial Empire is a brutal one, but the brutality has a thematic purpose. However, that doesn’t mean that the books are an unending parade of bleakness. Tahir also understands the importance of tenderness within such a harsh setting. The darker passages are all complemented by moments of affection and compassion that serve to make Laia and Elias’s resistance to the status quo matter all the more, especially as the scale and supernatural aspects of the plot increase.

You can purchase An Ember in the Ashes, the first novel in the An Ember in the Ashes quartet by Sabaa Tahir, here.

Humor is one of YA fantasy’s most underrated aspects, and no book series in the genre use it as effectively as Percy Jackson & the Olympians. Author Rick Riordan makes ancient gods hilariously fit the present-day world by translating the vanity, grudges, and family disputes that defined them in Ancient Greek myths into modern behavior. However, comedy isn’t the only reason Percy Jackson’s saga is now one of YA fiction's most iconic fantasy adventures. The series earns its place through the way it makes the emotional conflicts and problems faced by its young heroes while on their grand quest resonate perfectly with the target readership.

As Percy and his grow up across the 7 Percy Jackson novels, they must confront harsh truths like loyalty becoming more difficult when enemies have legitimate grievances, and that the journey to becoming a hero never comes without compromise or sacrifice. Its treatment of ADHD and dyslexia is especially memorable, reframing experiences associated with classroom frustration within an empowering fantasy framework. Rick Riordan never lets these ideas overwhelm the entertainment, either. The narrative voice remains conversational and quick, making exposition unusually painless and even enjoyable. It’s a perfect blend of lighthearted jokes, genuinely engaging fantasy adventure, and a core moral message that struggling to fit in never means one doesn’t matter.

You can purchase The Lightning Thief, the first novel in the Percy Jackson & the Olympians series by Rick Riordan, here.

The best urban fantasy novels depend on making familiar places feel newly charged with possibility, and The Mortal Instruments delivers that pleasure like few other YA book series. Nightclubs, streets, and buildings become entrances to a supernatural society with its own laws, prejudices, and competing loyalties. Beginning with City of Bones, Cassandra Clare’s six-book series follows teenager Clary as she discovers that she is a Shadowhunter, a human-angel hybrid. Clare builds outward from this premise to create a unique fantasy world that becomes the perfect setting to use fantasy conflict as a tool to examine emotional disorder and trauma.

The Mortal Instruments novels cover almost all the staple thematic topics associated with YA fantasy like friendships, romantic attachments, and complicated family histories. It’s how Cassandra Clare meshes them into a rich hidden fantasy world that incorporates dozens of supernatural species and cultures that makes the series a genre essential. While its unapologetically melodramatic tone does put some readers off, the way this intensity is used to explore ideas belonging and inherited prejudice is incredibly engaging. Even at their most extravagant, The Mortal Instruments remain among the most emotionally poignant YA fantasy series ever written, and they remain an absolute highlight of the wider genre.

You can purchase City of Bones, the first novel in The Mortal Instruments series by Cassandra Clare, here.

Philip Pullman’s His Dark Materials trilogy isn’t just a YA fantasy achievement, it’s a literary triumph. Not only is its fantasy worldbuilding unique and substantial and its approach to coming-of-age YA themes pitch-perfect, it’s also one of the most philosophically rich book trilogies of the modern era. The core of all three novels is the conflict between the free will of the individual and the assumed absolute authority of fate and destiny, with nearly every aspect and detail serving Pullman’s exploration. For example, the dæmons of protagonist Lyra’s world are much more than animal companions all humans are born with. They’re literal manifestations of the human soul, with their animal forms representing a person’s personality.

The fixed forms of these dæmons then naturally lead to questions surrounding whether someone’s characteristics are immutable, or whether they can eventually change. For a YA novel, this is extraordinary mature emotional territory, especially as the narrative unfolds and it becomes clear that Lyra and Will, the companion she finds in another world, may end up having to kill a figure who is god in all but name. Philip Pullman does a remarkable job of trusting young readers to engage with ideas like religious authority and ethical responsibility without ever talking down to them. At the same time, fantastical elements like armored bears, witches, and knives that can tear holes in reality ensure that the philosophical argument takes place within the confines of a riveting adventure.

You can purchase The Golden Compass, the first novel in the His Dark Materials trilogy by Philip Pullman, here.

While the world of The Hunger Games draws from dystopian sci-fi with its aesthetic, its story structure and the grand quest of the bow-and-arrow wielding Katniss Everdeen not only make it a perfect YA fantasy series, but one of the best in the entire genre. Author Suzanne Collins takes an immediately gripping survival premise and uses it to explore the role of entertainment in enforcing inequality and unjust political power. It’s a deeply relevant thematic focus for modern readers, especially compared with more traditional and morally clear-cut good vs. evil conflicts. It’s for this reason that The Hunger Games novels are, for many, the definitive example of YA fantasy at its most engaging.

However, there’s a lot more to The Hunger Games than simply tapping into the concerns of contemporary readers. The story is gripping throughout, and the way that Suzanne Collins refuses to treat the central rebellion as an inherent force-for-good that’s beyond scrutiny adds a moral complexity that ensures readers feel respected. Collins writes with a directness that makes these ideas accessible without making them simplistic. Combine this with the fact that the Games themselves make for some incredibly high-octane action sequences and Katniss being an incredibly well-written heroine, and The Hunger Games novels make their claim to being one of the best YA fantasy book series incredibly difficult to dispute.

You can purchase The Hunger Games, the first novel in The Hunger Games series by Suzanne Collins, here.

#3535. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.
